How to Use This Document

Paper 1 is a precision-recall paper: Section, Act, and case-name accuracy matter more than conceptual reasoning speed. Section A (Business Laws, 80%) tests four Acts by number and clause; Section B (Business Communication, 20%) is more conceptual but still tests exact terminology.

On question sourcing: ICMAI does not publish retrievable Foundation-level past papers. Every fact, formula, worked illustration and trap in this document is drawn exclusively from ICMAI's own published Study Notes for this paper (fetched directly during construction, including real case citations).

Exam Strategy — Precision-Recall Paper

1. No negative marking. Attempt all 50 — an educated elimination of two options costs nothing.

2. 72 seconds per question. Unlike calculation-heavy papers, most of that time here goes to recalling the RIGHT Section number, Act, or case name, not computing anything.

3. Distractors in this paper are usually a NEIGHBOURING Section or a similarly-named concept — a Void agreement instead of a Voidable one, Section 138 instead of Section 118, a Condition instead of a Warranty. Precision of terminology is the actual skill being tested.

4. Named pairs are the exam's favourite trap: Void vs Voidable, Condition vs Warranty, Promissory Note vs Bill of Exchange, General Crossing vs Special Crossing, Offer vs Invitation to Offer. Every such pair gets its own comparison table in this document.

MODULE ONE OF FIVE · SECTION A · 10% · ≈5 MCQs

Introduction

Sources of law, the legislative process, the court hierarchy and its jurisdictions, and the distinction between primary and subordinate legislation — the framework every later Act sits inside.

MUST NOT SKIP: the Supreme Court's five jurisdictions and the Article numbers behind Bills, Ordinances, and Amendments — the most Article-number-dense topic in the whole paper

5

Module Learning Objectives

After studying this module, you will be able to: know the development of the legal system in India over the years; understand the sources of law and the legislative process in India; develop an understanding of the court system in India; and know primary and subordinate legislation prevailing in India, with a brief introduction to alternative dispute resolution.

Glossary — Module 1, in Plain Words

The important legal and constitutional words from this module, explained simply.

StatuteA law formally passed by Parliament or a State Legislature — a written Act.
Judicial PrecedentA past court decision that later courts must follow when a similar case comes up again.
OrdinanceA law made directly by the President or a Governor when Parliament or the State Legislature isn't in session — a temporary, fast substitute for a normal law.
JurisdictionThe specific area of power or authority a court has — what kinds of cases it's allowed to decide.
WritA formal court order, used specifically to protect someone's Fundamental Rights.
Contempt (of court)Disobeying, disrespecting, or undermining a court's authority — something a court can punish directly.
SuperintendenceThe power to oversee and supervise lower courts or tribunals.
TribunalA special, more specialised type of court, usually dealing with one specific subject (tax, companies, environment) rather than general disputes.
Quasi-judicialActing somewhat like a court, but not being a full, formal court — e.g. a tribunal deciding disputes using court-like procedure.
ArbitrationA private way of settling a dispute, where an independent person (an arbitrator) decides the outcome instead of a court, and that decision is usually binding.
ConciliationA dispute-resolution process where a neutral person suggests a settlement, but it only becomes binding if BOTH sides agree to accept it.
MediationA neutral person helps two sides talk and find their own solution — the mediator never decides anything themselves.
Subordinate / Delegated LegislationDetailed rules made by a government department or local body, under permission given to it by a bigger law — not made by Parliament itself directly.
Ultra ViresA Latin phrase meaning "beyond the powers" — used when a rule or action goes further than what the law actually allowed.
RepealTo officially cancel or withdraw an existing law.
PromulgateTo formally announce and put a law (usually an ordinance) into effect.
CONCEPT

1.1 Sources of Law ★★ MED

H.L.A. Hart described law as “a set of rules.” In modern India, law derives from three broad sources: statutes, judicial precedents and customary law, and ordinances or regulations.

Four specific sources make up this picture in more detail, and each is worth understanding as its own distinct idea.

  1. Statutes are laws enacted by Parliament and by the State Legislatures, within the domains listed in the SEVENTH SCHEDULE of the Constitution — the Union List, the State List, and the Concurrent List. This includes every law passed both before and after the Constitution came into force in 1950, unless that law has been specifically repealed since.
  2. Judicial Precedents arise because Article 141 makes the law declared by the SUPREME COURT binding on ALL courts throughout India (in easy language: the Supreme Court and the High Courts don’t themselves write new laws the way Parliament does, but the way they interpret existing laws still functions as a genuine source of law that other courts must follow).
  3. Personal Laws are based on an individual’s own faith or community customs — examples include the Hindu Marriage Act 1955, the Indian Christian Marriage Act 1872, and the Kazis Act 1880.
  4. Ordinances and Regulations are recognised because Article 13(3)(a) defines “law” broadly enough to include any ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom, or usage that has the force of law. The PRESIDENT can promulgate ordinances under Article 123 when Parliament is not in session, and the GOVERNOR has a parallel power under Article 213 to do the same at the state level.

A Brief History of Indian Law, in Four Periods

The Ancient Period was governed by kingdom-specific law guided by the concept of “dharma,” drawing on texts such as the Vedas, the Smritis, the Upanishads, and the Arthasastra. Courts during this period were arranged in a clear hierarchy, rising from Kula, meaning family councils, through Shreni, meaning trade or professional councils, then Gana, the village assembly, then Adhikrita, a court appointed by the king, then Sasita, the king’s own court, and finally Nripa, the king himself as the ultimate authority.

The Medieval Period began in 1192 AD, when Mohammed Ghori defeated Prithviraj Chauhan, ushering in the Delhi Sultanate and later the Mughal courts. The Qazi-ul-Quzat was the chief judicial functionary of this era, assisted by the Mufti, who expounded the law, and the Mir Ad’l, who enforced the court’s decrees; the Qadi-e-Askar handled military justice, functioning much like today’s Court Martial.

The British Administrative Period lasted roughly 200 years, and packed in a great many distinct developments worth listing individually.

  • The Charter of Elizabeth in 1600 first empowered limited legislative rights in India.
  • The Battle of Plassey in 1757, followed by the 1765 grant of Dewani rights in Bengal, shifted the East India Company decisively toward genuine administrative power.
  • The Mayor’s Court was established in 1726.
  • Warren Hastings introduced the Adalat System in 1772.
  • The Indian High Courts Act of 1861 established High Courts at Calcutta, Madras, and Bombay.
  • The Government of India Act of 1935 was accompanied by the establishment of the Federal Court in 1937.
  • This era also produced three foundational statutes that remain significant today: the Indian Penal Code of 1860, the Indian Contract Act of 1872, and the Indian Evidence Act of 1872 — the Contract Act was later split apart, giving rise to the separate Sale of Goods Act of 1930 and the Indian Partnership Act of 1932.

The Indian Legal Period runs from 1950 to the present day, beginning with the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949. The Drafting Committee, chaired by Mr. B.R. Ambedkar from 29 August 1947, produced the Constitution that was passed and adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949, a date still celebrated as Law Day, before being formally brought into force on 26 January 1950.

⚡ SHORTCUT: Article 123=PRESIDENT's ordinance power; Article 213=GOVERNOR's ordinance power (state-level mirror); Article 141=Supreme Court's precedent binds ALL courts — these three Article numbers are tested directly and repeatedly.

Concept Check 1 — Identifying the Source of Law

GIVEN: Classify the source of law in each case: (a) the Indian Contract Act, 1872, enacted by Parliament; (b) a Supreme Court ruling on the interpretation of "consideration" that all lower courts must now follow; (c) the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, governing marriage among Hindus.

STEP 1: (a) enacted directly by the legislature → Statute.

STEP 2: (b) a court interpretation binding on all courts under Article 141 → Judicial Precedent.

STEP 3: (c) faith/custom-based law for a specific community → Personal Law.

ANSWER: (a) Statute, (b) Judicial Precedent (Article 141), (c) Personal Law.

MCQ NOTE: distractor calls (c) a "statute" since it was formally enacted by Parliament — but the exam's classification of Personal Law is by SUBJECT MATTER (faith/custom-governed, community-specific), not by whether Parliament happened to codify it; the Hindu Marriage Act is a statute AND a personal law simultaneously, and this question type usually wants the personal-law classification specifically.

CONCEPT

1.2 Legislative Process in India ★★★ HIGH

India has a two-tier federal structure — affirmed by the Supreme Court in S.R. Bommai vs Union of India (1994) — but with a unitary bias strong enough that it is often described as “quasi-federal.” There are TWO major law-making bodies in this structure: Parliament at the Union level, and the State Legislature at the state level.

Six distinct ideas together explain how this legislative process actually works, and each deserves to be read as its own complete point.

  1. Under Article 79, Parliament consists of the President together with the Rajya Sabha, also called the Council of States, and the Lok Sabha, also called the House of the People. Under Article 168, the State Legislature consists of the Governor together with one House, the Legislative Assembly, or in some states, two Houses, the Legislative Assembly and the Legislative Council.
  2. On the power to legislate, Article 245 gives Parliament the power to make laws for all or part of India, and gives State Legislatures the power to make laws for all or part of their own State. Article 246, read together with the SEVENTH SCHEDULE, splits legislative subjects into three lists: the Union List, which is Parliament’s exclusive domain, the State List, which is the State’s exclusive domain, and the Concurrent List, on which both Parliament and the States may legislate.
  3. On resolving conflicts, Article 254 provides that if a State law conflicts with a Parliament law on a Concurrent List subject, the PARLIAMENT law prevails — unless the State law had been reserved for the President’s consideration and actually received Presidential assent.
  4. On introducing a Bill, Article 107 allows a Bill to originate in EITHER House of Parliament, except for Money Bills, which under Article 109 can start ONLY in the Lok Sabha. A Bill introduced by a Minister is called a Government Bill, while a Bill introduced by anyone else is called a Private Member’s Bill.
  5. On ordinances, the President’s power under Article 123, and the Governor’s parallel power under Article 213, can only be used when the relevant House or Houses are NOT currently in session. The tenure of an ordinance can vary from six weeks to six months, depending on the circumstances. Article 243 extends this same idea of power-sharing a step further, down to local rural governance under the Panchayati Raj system.
  6. On amending the Constitution, Article 368 gives Parliament the power to amend it by addition, variation, or repeal — but the Supreme Court held in Keshavananda Bharati vs State of Kerala (1973) that any amendment which is in contravention of the Fundamental Rights of an individual will itself be unconstitutional.
⚡ SHORTCUT: Article 107=Bill introduction; Article 109=Money Bill starts in Lok Sabha only; Article 245/246=power to legislate; Article 254=Parliament wins a Union-State conflict; Article 368=amendment power, bounded by the rule that an amendment contravening Fundamental Rights is unconstitutional (Keshavananda Bharati, 1973).

Concept Check 2 — Matching Articles to Their Legislative Function

GIVEN: Match each function to its Constitutional Article: (a) a Money Bill can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha; (b) Parliament's law prevails over a conflicting State law on a Concurrent List subject; (c) Parliament may amend the Constitution by addition, variation, or repeal.

STEP 1: (a) Money Bill restriction → Article 109.

STEP 2: (b) Union-State law conflict resolution → Article 254.

STEP 3: (c) Constitutional amendment power → Article 368.

ANSWER: (a) Article 109, (b) Article 254, (c) Article 368.

MCQ NOTE: distractor swaps (a) with Article 107 — Article 107 covers Bills GENERALLY (originate in either House); Article 109 is the SPECIFIC exception carved out for Money Bills. When a question mentions "Money Bill" specifically, the answer is 109, not the general 107.

CONCEPT

1.3 Legal Method & Court System in India ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

India has a single integrated, pyramidal judicial system: the Supreme Court sits at the apex, High Courts sit at the state level below it, and Subordinate Courts sit below the High Courts. This structure is established under Part V, Chapter IV of the Constitution for the Supreme Court, and Part VI, Chapters V and VI, for the High Courts and Subordinate Courts respectively.

The Supreme Court [Articles 124–147]

The Supreme Court was established on 26 January 1950 under Article 124(1), with 8 judges originally, and currently has 34, made up of 33 judges plus the Chief Justice. It exercises five distinct jurisdictions.

  1. The ORIGINAL jurisdiction, under Article 131, covers disputes between the Union and the States, or between States themselves.
  2. The WRIT jurisdiction, under Article 32, provides a remedy for the violation of Fundamental Rights guaranteed under Part III of the Constitution.
  3. The APPELLATE jurisdiction allows the Supreme Court to hear appeals from High Court orders.
  4. The ADVISORY jurisdiction allows the Supreme Court to advise the President on questions of public importance.
  5. The power to punish for CONTEMPT is given to the Supreme Court under Article 129, and to the High Courts under Article 215; the Supreme Court also has a REVIEW jurisdiction under Article 137, allowing it to review its own earlier orders.

The High Court

  • The High Court has original jurisdiction over the enforcement of Fundamental Rights, election disputes, and revenue matters.
  • Its WRIT jurisdiction, under Article 226, is actually WIDER than the Supreme Court’s own writ power under Article 32, since it covers both Fundamental Rights AND ordinary legal rights, not Fundamental Rights alone.
  • It has appellate jurisdiction over the subordinate courts within its territory.
  • It has the power of SUPERINTENDENCE over all courts and tribunals within its territory, under Article 227, and the power to transfer to itself any case that raises a substantial question of law, under Article 228.
  • It is also a Court of Record with its own contempt power, under Article 215.

Subordinate Courts — Criminal and Civil Branches

Under Section 6 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, the CRIMINAL branch of subordinate courts is arranged in a hierarchy: the Court of Session, headed by a Sessions Judge, who can pass any punishment except the death penalty without needing High Court confirmation, sits above the Court of Metropolitan Magistrate, which operates in areas with a population over 1 million, which in turn sits above the Court of Chief Judicial Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the First or Second Class. Executive Magistrates also exist within this system, but they are administrative officials, not judicial ones.

The CIVIL branch is arranged separately: the District Court is the highest civil court within a district, with its judges appointed by the Governor under Article 233, sitting above the Sub-Judge, who in turn sits above the Additional Sub-Judge, with Munsif Courts at the base of this hierarchy.

Tribunals

Tribunals are quasi-judicial bodies set up to handle specialised or technical matters, and they mix judicial members with technical members on their bench. Only persons with a genuine judicial background — meaning former High Court judges, or lawyers who are themselves eligible for appointment to a High Court — may serve as Judicial Members on a tribunal. The Tribunals Reforms (Rationalisation and Conditions of Service) Ordinance, 2021, abolished nine separate tribunals, transferring their functions directly to the High Courts.

Alternative Dispute Resolution

Section 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, allows a court to refer a case to any of four recognised alternative dispute resolution mechanisms, and each works quite differently from the others.

  1. Arbitration results in a binding “award” handed down by an arbitral tribunal, with only minimal scope for judicial intervention afterward.
  2. Conciliation produces only a non-binding recommendation, which becomes binding only if BOTH parties actively accept it.
  3. Mediation involves a mediator who facilitates discussion between the parties, but does not themselves decide the outcome.
  4. Lok Adalat, operating under the Legal Services Authority Act, 1987, issues an order that is deemed to be a civil court decree — it is final and is NOT appealable.

The two governing statutes for these mechanisms are the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, and the Legal Services Authority Act, 1987. Several other statutes go further and make mediation a COMPULSORY step before a suit can even be filed.

  • The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, requires it under Section 4.
  • The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, requires it for pending cases and family matters, following a 2002 amendment.
  • The Companies Act, 2013, requires it under Section 442.
  • The MSME Development Act, 2006, requires it under Section 18.
  • The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, requires it under Section 32(g).
  • The Commercial Courts Act, 2015, following a 2018 amendment, only allows litigation after a meaningful attempt at mediation has already failed.
  • The Consumer Protection Act, 2019, requires mediation to be attempted before approaching a redressal agency.

The main advantages of these alternative mechanisms are that they are less time-consuming and more cost-effective than ordinary litigation.

⚡ SHORTCUT: Article 32=Supreme Court writ (Fundamental Rights only); Article 226=High Court writ (Fundamental Rights + legal rights, hence WIDER); Article 131=Supreme Court original jurisdiction (Union-State disputes); Article 137=Supreme Court reviewing its OWN orders — four numbers covering four distinct jobs.
CONCEPT

1.3 (cont’d) Regulatory Bodies in India ★★★ HIGH

Seven key regulatory bodies oversee different parts of India’s financial and administrative landscape, and each has its own distinct scope worth learning separately.

  1. SEBI, established under the SEBI Act, 1992, protects investors and prevents malpractice such as insider trading and price rigging, regulating capital markets through protective, regulatory, and development functions; it can change stock-exchange rules, access exchange records, and approve or force delisting.
  2. RBI, established under the RBI Act, 1935, is India’s central bank; it licenses banks, sets prudential norms under the Basel framework, manages reserve ratios, prints currency, and manages foreign exchange under FEMA 1999.
  3. IRDAI, established under the IRDA Act, 1999, protects policyholders, regulates insurers’ financial soundness, and sets premium and conduct standards.
  4. PFRDA, established under the PFRDA Act, 2013, is the sole regulator of the pension industry, managing the National Pension System, which has been extended from government employees to all citizens, including NRIs.
  5. AMFI, set up in 1995, is a self-regulatory, non-profit body for the mutual fund industry, functioning as a division of SEBI; it updates the Net Asset Value of funds daily.
  6. MCA, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, administers the Companies Act 1956 and 2013 through the Registrar of Companies.
  7. NHB, established under the National Housing Bank Act, 1987, on 9 July 1988, is the apex regulator for housing finance companies, operating under the Ministry of Finance.
⚡ SHORTCUT: SEBI=capital markets (1992); RBI=banking/currency (1935, oldest); IRDAI=insurance (1999); PFRDA=pensions (2013); AMFI=mutual funds, a SEBI division (1995, self-regulatory not statutory); MCA=companies; NHB=housing finance (1987).
CONCEPT

1.4 Primary & Subordinate Legislation ★★ MED

Primary Legislation derives directly from Parliament or State Legislature enactments, along with the limited Presidential and Gubernatorial power to issue ordinances. Subordinate Legislation, also called Secondary or Delegated Legislation, is instead made by an authority to whom the legislature has DELEGATED law-making power, and it can never legally exceed the scope of that delegation.

Four ideas together explain how and why subordinate legislation exists, and each deserves to be read as its own point.

  1. Subordinate legislation exists because legislatures, constrained by limited time, cannot realistically handle every technical or local detail themselves; the Supreme Court, in Gwalior Rayon Mills Mfg. Co. Ltd. vs Assistant Commissioner of Sales Tax, held that delegated legislation exists precisely to obtain “flexibility, elasticity, expedition and opportunity for experimentation.”
  2. Subordinate legislation takes the FORM of rules, regulations, and bye-laws, made by the Central Government, State Governments, and local authorities under power conferred or delegated to them by the legislature. Article 312 illustrates this directly: if the Rajya Sabha resolves, by a two-thirds majority, that it is necessary in the national interest, Parliament may create new All India Services — the IAS and IPS are themselves deemed to have been created under this very Article.
  3. The critical limit on all of this is that subordinate legislation CANNOT go beyond the parent Act or the Constitution itself; any subordinate legislation that transgresses the Act’s own scope, or the Constitution, can be struck down as ULTRA VIRES, meaning “beyond the powers” granted.
  4. LOCAL GOVERNANCE is one of the LARGEST sources of subordinate legislation, since local regulations often need very rapid revision. Part IX of the Constitution covers the Panchayat system, and Part IXA covers Municipalities. The COVID-19 pandemic illustrated exactly why this matters: rapidly-changing, localised guidelines would have been impossibly slow to enact if they had to go through Parliament or a State Legislature directly each time.
⚡ SHORTCUT: Primary Legislation = made BY the legislature itself. Subordinate Legislation = made by someone the legislature DELEGATED power to, and it's automatically void the moment it steps outside that delegated scope ("ultra vires").

Concept Check 3 — Primary or Subordinate Legislation?

GIVEN: Classify each: (a) the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, passed by Parliament; (b) a municipal bye-law regulating waste collection timings in a city, made under powers delegated by the State Legislature; (c) a Presidential Ordinance issued while Parliament is not in session.

STEP 1: (a) direct parliamentary enactment → Primary Legislation.

STEP 2: (b) made by a LOCAL AUTHORITY under delegated power → Subordinate Legislation.

STEP 3: (c) issued directly by the President under Article 123, treated with the force of law → Primary Legislation (an exercise of the President's own constitutionally-granted emergency power, not a delegation to a subordinate body).

ANSWER: (a) Primary, (b) Subordinate, (c) Primary.

MCQ NOTE: distractor calls (c) "Subordinate" reasoning that an Ordinance isn't a full Act passed by Parliament — but the President's ordinance power comes directly from the CONSTITUTION (Article 123), not from a delegation by Parliament, which is exactly why it counts as Primary rather than Subordinate legislation.

Module 1 — Trap Analysis

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: ARTICLE 32 AND ARTICLE 226 SWAPPED

THE TRAP: a question naming the SUPREME COURT's writ power gets answered "Article 226," or a question naming the HIGH COURT's writ power gets answered "Article 32."

THE TWIST: Article 32 is the Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction, limited to FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS violations only. Article 226 is the High Court's writ jurisdiction, and is WIDER — it covers Fundamental Rights AND ordinary legal rights.

WHY IT FOOLS: both are "writ jurisdiction" articles doing a similar job at different court levels, and the numbers themselves give no intuitive clue about which court they belong to.

THE FIX: "32" and "Supreme Court" pair together; "226" and "High Court" pair together — and remember 226 is the BROADER power, since High Courts also protect ordinary legal rights that Article 32 doesn't reach.

MEMORY HOOK: "32 is SMALL in number and SMALL in scope (Fundamental Rights only) — Supreme Court. 226 is the BIGGER number and the BIGGER scope — High Court."

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: PRESIDENT'S AND GOVERNOR'S ORDINANCE ARTICLES SWAPPED

THE TRAP: Article 123 (President) and Article 213 (Governor) are treated as interchangeable since both describe near-identical ordinance powers.

THE TWIST: Article 123 is specifically the PRESIDENT's power, exercised when PARLIAMENT is not in session, with effect across India (or the relevant part). Article 213 is the GOVERNOR's mirrored power for a STATE, exercised when the STATE LEGISLATURE is not in session, with effect limited to that state's territory.

WHY IT FOOLS: the two powers are structurally near-identical (same trigger condition, same type of instrument), differing only in WHO holds them and at WHICH level.

THE FIX: "President" and "Parliament not in session" → Article 123. "Governor" and "State Legislature not in session" → Article 213.

MEMORY HOOK: "123 is the President's — as basic and central as counting 1-2-3. 213 is the Governor's state-level mirror."

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: JUDICIAL PRECEDENT ARTICLE CONFUSED WITH AMENDMENT ARTICLE

THE TRAP: Article 141 (Supreme Court precedent binding on all courts) and Article 368 (Parliament's power to amend the Constitution) get confused since both concern the Constitution's ongoing authority.

THE TWIST: Article 141 is about the COURT's interpretive power binding future cases — a source of LAW through precedent. Article 368 is about the LEGISLATURE's power to literally change the Constitution's text — a source of CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT, not judicial interpretation.

WHY IT FOOLS: both articles describe a kind of "authority that shapes future law," making them easy to blur without checking WHO holds the power (court vs legislature).

THE FIX: "binding on all COURTS" and "judicial precedent" → Article 141. "Amend/add/vary/repeal the Constitution" → Article 368.

MEMORY HOOK: "141: courts follow the COURT. 368: Parliament changes the CONSTITUTION itself."

Module 1 — Comparison Tables

JurisdictionArticleWhat It Covers
OriginalArticle 131Union-State or State-State disputes
WritArticle 32Fundamental Rights violations only
Appellate—Appeals from High Court orders
Advisory—Advises the President on public-importance questions
ReviewArticle 137Reviewing the Court's own past orders
ContemptArticle 129Punishing contempt of itself (Article 215 = same power for High Courts)
★ EXAM TRICK: the Supreme Court has FIVE distinct named jurisdictions plus a separate review power — questions often test which single Article number matches which named jurisdiction.
BasisSupreme Court (Art. 32)High Court (Art. 226)
Rights coveredFundamental Rights onlyFundamental Rights + ordinary legal rights
ScopeNarrowerWider
Territorial reachAll of IndiaThe Court's own state/territory
★ EXAM TRICK: Article 226 is deliberately WIDER than Article 32 — a common wrong-answer instinct assumes the Supreme Court's power must always be "bigger," but on writs specifically, the High Court's reach is broader.
12 EXAM FACTS — INTRODUCTION

① Article 141: Supreme Court precedent binds ALL courts in India.

② Article 123: President's ordinance power. Article 213: Governor's mirrored power at state level.

③ Article 79: Parliament = President + Rajya Sabha + Lok Sabha. Article 168: State Legislature = Governor + Assembly (+ Council in some states).

④ Article 109: Money Bills start ONLY in the Lok Sabha. Article 107: ordinary Bills may start in either House.

⑤ Article 254: Parliament's law prevails over a conflicting State law on a Concurrent List subject.

⑥ Article 368: Constitutional amendment power — limited by the "basic structure" doctrine (Keshavananda Bharati, 1973).

⑦ Article 32 = Supreme Court writ (Fundamental Rights only). Article 226 = High Court writ (wider — Fundamental + legal rights).

⑧ Article 131 = Supreme Court Original Jurisdiction. Article 137 = Supreme Court Review Jurisdiction (its own orders).

⑨ District Court = highest CIVIL court in a district; Sessions Court = top of the CRIMINAL hierarchy at that level.

⑩ Executive Magistrates are administrative, NOT judicial officers.

⑪ Lok Adalat orders are final, deemed civil-court decrees, and NOT appealable — unique among ADR methods.

⑫ Subordinate legislation is void the moment it exceeds its parent Act or the Constitution — the "ultra vires" test.

MODULE TWO OF FIVE · SECTION A · 30% · ≈15 MCQs

Indian Contract
Act, 1872

Essential elements and types of contract, offer and acceptance, void/voidable agreements, consideration, capacity and free consent, quasi/contingent contracts, performance, indemnity/guarantee/pledge/agency, e-contracts, discharge, and breach — the single largest module in the paper, built directly from the ICMAI Study Notes.

MUST NOT SKIP: Void vs Voidable, and the landmark cases (Carlill, Balfour vs Balfour, Mohiri Bibi vs Dharmodas Ghose) — the most repeated question type in this module

15

Module Learning Objectives

After studying this module, you will be able to: know the essential elements of a contract; understand the difference between a void and a voidable contract; appreciate the importance of consideration in a contract; know the capacity of parties to a contract and the importance of free consent; understand the meaning of Indemnity, Guarantee, Pledge, and Agent; understand the meaning of performance of a contract; appreciate the meaning and requirements of e-contracts and e-signatures; know the various modes of discharging a contract; and develop an understanding of breach of contract and remedies for the same.

Glossary — Module 2, in Plain Words

The important legal words from this module, explained simply.

Promisor / PromiseePromisor = the person making a promise. Promisee = the person the promise is made TO.
ConsiderationWhat each side gives or gets in return — usually money, but can also be a favour, a service, or a promise to do (or not do) something.
Void / VoidableVoid = has no legal effect at all, as if it never happened. Voidable = still stands, but one side has the CHOICE to cancel it if they want to.
Ab initioA Latin phrase meaning "from the very beginning" — used to say something was never valid, right from the start.
Consensus ad idemA Latin phrase meaning "agreement on the same thing" — both people understanding the deal in exactly the same way.
CoercionForcing someone into an agreement through an illegal act or threat.
Undue InfluenceUsing a position of power or trust over someone (like a guru over a disciple) to unfairly pressure them into an agreement.
FraudDeliberately lying, or deliberately hiding the truth, to trick someone into an agreement.
MisrepresentationSaying something false, but genuinely (innocently) believing it was true.
IndemnityA promise to cover someone's loss or damage if something goes wrong.
Guarantee / SuretyGuarantee = a promise to pay or perform if a THIRD person fails to. Surety = the person who makes that promise on the third person's behalf.
Pledge / Pawnor / PawneePledge = handing over goods as security for a loan. Pawnor = the person giving the goods. Pawnee = the person holding them as security.
Agent / PrincipalAgent = a person who acts on someone else's behalf. Principal = the person the agent is acting for.
NovationSwapping out an old contract for a brand-new one, usually because a party or a term has changed.
RescissionSimply cancelling a contract.
RemissionThe person owed something agrees to accept LESS than what was originally promised.
RepudiationRefusing to go ahead with a contract, or making it clear in advance that you won't perform it.
DamagesMoney awarded by a court to compensate someone for a loss they suffered.
InjunctionA court order telling someone NOT to do something.
Quantum MeruitA Latin phrase meaning "as much as is earned" — paying someone fairly for the work they've actually done so far.
CONCEPT

2.1 Essential Elements, Types of Contract, Offer & Acceptance ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Section 2(h): "an agreement enforceable by law." Section 2(e): "every promise and every set of promises forming consideration for each other." Agreement = Offer + Acceptance; Contract = Agreement + Enforceability by Law.

The Act's original structure: four parts — general principles of contract [Sec 1-75], sale of goods [Sec 76-123, later repealed and separated into the Sale of Goods Act, 1930], special contracts [Sec 124-238], and partnership [later repealed into the Partnership Act, 1932].

Key definitions:

  • 2(a) Proposal/Offer.
  • 2(b) Acceptance — an accepted proposal becomes a promise.
  • 2(c) Promisor/Promisee.
  • 2(d) Consideration.
  • 2(f) Reciprocal Promises.
  • 2(g) Void Agreement.
  • 2(i) Voidable Contract.
  • 2(j) Void Contract.

Ten essential elements (Section 10):

  1. Agreement.
  2. Free Consent [Sec 14].
  3. Lawful Consideration.
  4. Competent Parties (18+, sound mind, not disqualified).
  5. Legality of Object.
  6. Intention to create LEGAL relationship — BALFOUR vs BALFOUR: a husband's monthly allowance promise to his wife was held outside the realm of contract altogether, being purely domestic; similarly a father's promise to pay his son ₹1 lakh for passing CA in the first attempt was held unenforceable as a domestic-nature agreement.
  7. Not expressly declared void.
  8. Consensus ad idem — A owns a Hero Honda and a Bajaj Pulsar; he offers to sell "his Pulsar" without naming it; B, thinking he means the Hero Honda, accepts — no agreement forms, since there's no meeting of minds.
  9. Certain and capable of performance.
  10. Legal formalities where required by the nature of the agreement.
Balfour vs Balfour — A husband's promise of a monthly household allowance to his wife was held outside the realm of contract altogether — purely domestic arrangements lack the intention to create legal relations.

Concept Check 1 — Identifying the Missing Essential Element

GIVEN: (a) A invites B, a film actor, to his daughter's engagement dinner; B accepts but doesn't turn up; A wants to sue for the wasted special arrangements. (b) A has a Hero Honda and a Bajaj Pulsar; he offers to sell "his Pulsar" without naming it; B, thinking he means the Hero Honda, accepts.

STEP 1: (a) a social invitation, however formally arranged, lacks the intention to create a legal relationship — A cannot sue B.

STEP 2: (b) A and B are thinking of two different motorcycles — no consensus ad idem exists.

ANSWER: (a) Missing intention to create legal relations (a social agreement). (b) Missing consensus ad idem.

MCQ NOTE: distractor calls (a) a free-consent problem — but free consent (Sec 14) concerns defects in an agreement that DOES exist; here, no legally-intended agreement was ever on the table at all, since social/domestic arrangements are outside contract law's scope entirely.

CONCEPT

2.1 (cont'd) Types of Contract ★★★ HIGH

By enforceability:

  • Valid — satisfies Sec 10 in full.
  • Void Agreement [2(g)] — void ab initio, e.g. Kamala promises to lend Ramesh money in exchange for Ramesh getting Kamala's own (existing) marriage dissolved so he can marry her himself.
  • Voidable [2(i)].
  • Void Contract [2(j)] — valid at formation, later unenforceable, e.g. two countries' citizens contract to trade, then war breaks out between their countries.
  • Unenforceable — technical defect, e.g. missing writing.
  • Illegal — narrower than void: all illegal agreements are void, but not all void agreements are illegal.

By formation: Formal (validity depends on form, not consideration — under seal, or of record) vs Simple/Parol. By performance: Executed (fully completed both sides) vs Executory. By obligation: Unilateral (only one party owes a future obligation once concluded — e.g. a railway ticket booked in advance) vs Bilateral vs Multilateral (more than two parties, often international). By creation [Sec 9]: Express (words, spoken or written) vs Implied (conduct, not words — e.g. boarding a public bus implies an offer by the transport company; inserting coins into a platform-ticket vending machine is acceptance of the machine owner's implied offer).

Concept Check 2 — Classifying Contract Types

GIVEN: (a) A and B, citizens of different countries, contract to trade; war breaks out between their countries before performance. (b) A books a railway ticket for travel a month later. (c) Ramamurthy, an Indian citizen, contracts with a friendly alien.

STEP 1: (a) valid at formation, later unenforceable due to war → Void Contract.

STEP 2: (b) only the railway owes a future obligation once booked → Unilateral Contract.

STEP 3: (c) a contract with a friendly alien (not an alien ENEMY) is fully valid.

ANSWER: (a) Void Contract, (b) Unilateral Contract, (c) Valid Contract.

MCQ NOTE: distractor calls (a) a "Void Agreement" — Void Agreements are void from birth; here the contract was genuinely valid until war intervened later, which is exactly the Void Contract distinction.

CONCEPT

2.1 (cont'd) Offer & Acceptance ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Types of offer: Specific (to a definite person) vs General — CARLILL vs CARBOLIC SMOKE BALL CO.: a company advertised a £100 reward to anyone catching influenza despite using its product as directed; Mrs Carlill did so and claimed the reward; held, compliance with a general offer's terms IS acceptance, she could recover. Cross Offer (two identical offers crossing in ignorance — no contract forms). Counter Offer (different terms proposed — kills the original offer).

Offer vs Invitation to Offer: an offer binds the moment it's accepted; an invitation to offer merely invites others to make an offer. Goods displayed with price tags, advertisements, and auction catalogues are invitations to offer. A bids at a public auction — this is merely an offer by the bidder; no concluded contract exists until the auctioneer accepts, by the fall of the hammer or similar customary method.

Essentials of Valid Acceptance [Sec 7]: must be ABSOLUTE and UNQUALIFIED; must be communicated in the offeror's prescribed mode, or a reasonable mode if none is prescribed. Acceptance must be COMMUNICATED — silence is never acceptance.

FELTHOUSE vs BINDLEY: an uncle wrote to his nephew offering to buy a horse, adding "if I hear no more, I shall consider the horse mine"; the nephew never replied but told an auctioneer not to sell it; the auctioneer sold it by mistake; held, silence cannot constitute acceptance, no contract existed.

FOSTER vs MACKINNON: a person endorsed a bill of exchange believing it to be a guarantee; held, his mind never went with the writing, so no consent existed — void ab initio.

⚡ SHORTCUT: "Silence = acceptance" is NEVER valid in Indian contract law, even if the offeror tries to impose it unilaterally (Felthouse vs Bindley).
Carlill vs Carbolic Smoke Ball Co. — Compliance with the terms of a general offer to the public itself constitutes acceptance.

Concept Check 3 — Offer vs Invitation to Offer

GIVEN: (a) A puts three one-rupee coins in the slot of a platform-ticket vending machine at a railway station. (b) A bids at a public auction. (c) A shop displays a jacket with a price tag.

STEP 1: (a) inserting the coins is acceptance of the vending machine owner's standing implied offer — a valid contract forms immediately.

STEP 2: (b) A's bid is merely an offer — no contract exists until the auctioneer accepts (e.g. fall of the hammer).

STEP 3: (c) the displayed, priced jacket is an Invitation to Offer, not an Offer.

ANSWER: (a) Offer, accepted by inserting coins. (b) A's bid is an Offer, not yet accepted. (c) Invitation to Offer.

MCQ NOTE: distractor treats (a) as merely an invitation like (c) — but a stocked, ready-to-transact vending machine is a recognised exception where the machine owner is treated as making a genuine standing offer, since no further negotiation step remains.

CONCEPT

2.2 Void & Voidable Agreements, No Consideration No Contract ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Voidable Contract [Sec 2(i)]: enforceable at the option of one or more parties, but not the other — typically because free consent was absent (e.g. A compels B by force to sign an agreement — voidable at B's option). Void Agreement [Sec 2(g)]: never enforceable, null and void ab initio. Void Contract [Sec 2(j)]: valid at first, later ceases to be enforceable.

Thirteen categories the Act expressly declares void:

  1. Agreement by a minor or unsound-mind person [Sec 11, 12].
  2. Unlawful consideration/object [Sec 23].
  3. Bilateral mistake of fact material to the agreement [Sec 20].
  4. Consideration/object unlawful in PART, inseparable from the legal part [Sec 24].
  5. No consideration [Sec 25].
  6. Restraint of marriage, except a minor's [Sec 26].
  7. Restraint of trade — exception: sale of goodwill [Sec 27].
  8. Restraint of legal proceedings [Sec 28].
  9. Uncertain meaning [Sec 29].
  10. Wager [Sec 30].
  11. Contingent on an impossible event [Sec 36].
  12. Agreement to do an impossible act [Sec 56].
  13. Reciprocal promises, part legal part illegal — the illegal part is void [Sec 57].
⚡ SHORTCUT: Thirteen numbered categories, Sections 11/12 → 23 → 20 → 24 → 25 → 26 → 27 → 28 → 29 → 30 → 36 → 56 → 57 — a genuinely memorisable sequence once you see it as one continuous list rather than scattered facts.

Concept Check 4 — Which Section Voids This Agreement?

GIVEN: (a) Ram sells the goodwill of his shop to Shyam for ₹4,00,000 and separately promises never to carry on such business, forever, anywhere in India. (b) Prakash and Girish agree they will never institute legal proceedings against each other without mutual consent. (c) Sohan agrees to sell Mohan his black horse; unknown to both, the horse was already dead at the time of the agreement.

STEP 1: (a) the goodwill-sale exception under Sec 27 exists, but an unlimited, worldwide, lifetime restraint goes beyond reasonable scope → void, Sec 27.

STEP 2: (b) a blanket bar on ever approaching a court → void, Sec 28 (restraint of legal proceedings).

STEP 3: (c) both parties mistaken about the existence of the very subject matter → void, Sec 20 (bilateral mistake of fact).

ANSWER: (a) Section 27, (b) Section 28, (c) Section 20.

CONCEPT

2.3 Consideration, Legality of Object & Consideration ★★★ HIGH

Section 2(d): consideration is something done, abstained from, or promised, at the promisor's desire, by the promisee OR ANY OTHER PERSON.

Six legal rules of consideration:

  1. Must move at the promisor's DESIRE, not a third party's — DURGA PRASAD vs BALDEO: D built a market at a District Collector's instance; shop occupants promised D a commission; held, no consideration, since the spending was at the Collector's (a third party's) request, not the promisee's — void. NATIONAL BANK OF UPPER INDIA vs BANSIDHAR: C promised to pay B on A's behalf; B credited A's account on faith of C's promise — held, the discharge of A's account WAS valid consideration for C's promise.
  2. May move from the promisee OR ANY OTHER PERSON — CHINNAYYA vs RAMAYYA: A gifted property to her daughter, directing the daughter pay an annuity to A's brother; the daughter later refused, claiming no consideration moved from the uncle; held, Sec 2(d)'s phrase "promisee or any other person" means consideration need not move from the promisee — the uncle could sue.
  3. Need not be adequate — COLLINS vs GODFREY: a witness paid beyond statutory expenses for appearing at trial has no valid consideration, since he was already legally bound to appear; inadequacy alone doesn't void a contract, though courts may weigh it as evidence toward a free-consent question.
  4. May be an act, abstinence, or return promise.
  5. May be PAST, PRESENT, or FUTURE (a genuine departure from English law, where past consideration is no consideration) — SINDHE vs ABRAHAM: services rendered to a minor at his own request, continuing after majority at his renewed request, followed by a promise to pay an annuity — held, valid past consideration.
  6. Must not be unlawful [Sec 23 — forbidden by law, defeats any law's provisions, fraudulent, injures person/property, or immoral/against public policy].

No Consideration, No Contract [Sec 25] — SEVEN exceptions:

  1. Natural love and affection, written and registered, between near relatives [Sec 25(1)].
  2. Promise to compensate for a past voluntary act [Sec 25(2)].
  3. A written, signed promise to pay a time-barred debt [Sec 25(3)].
  4. Completed gifts [Explanation 1 to Sec 25].
  5. Creation of agency [Sec 185].
  6. Contract of guarantee [Sec 127].
  7. Remission [Sec 63].
⚡ SHORTCUT: Seven Section-25 exceptions, not three — a very common under-count. Love/affection, past voluntary act, time-barred debt, completed gifts, agency creation, guarantee, remission.
Chinnayya vs Ramayya — Consideration can move from any person, not only the promisee — Section 2(d)'s exact wording ("promisee or any other person") was the deciding text.
Kedarnath vs Gorie Mohammad — a defendant had agreed to subscribe ₹100 towards building a Town Hall; on the faith of that promise, the plaintiff-secretary called for construction plans and entrusted the work to contractors, undertaking personal liability to them; held, the promise was enforceable, since the secretary's own detriment — undertaking liability to the contractors on the faith of the subscription promise — itself constituted valid consideration.

Concept Check 5 — Is the Consideration Valid?

GIVEN: (a) D builds a market at a District Collector's instance; shop occupants later promise D a commission on sales. (b) K promises to sell a house worth ₹8 lakh for just ₹2 lakh, both parties freely consenting. (c) A renders services to B at B's request; B later promises payment for those already-completed services.

STEP 1: (a) the expenditure was at a THIRD PARTY's (Collector's) desire, not the promisee's → no valid consideration.

STEP 2: (b) mere inadequacy doesn't void a freely-consented agreement → valid.

STEP 3: (c) past consideration, rendered at the promisor's own prior request → valid under Indian law.

ANSWER: (a) Not valid consideration (Durga Prasad vs Baldeo). (b) Valid. (c) Valid (past consideration).

CONCEPT

2.4 Capacity of Parties, Free Consent ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act tells us who is legally competent to enter into a contract: a person must have attained the age of majority, must be of sound mind, and must not be disqualified from contracting by any other law that applies to them (in easy language: the law only lets you sign a valid contract if you are old enough, mentally fit, and not specifically barred by some other rule). The Act then lists three categories of people who are NOT competent to contract: minors, persons of unsound mind, and persons disqualified by some other law.

Who Is a Minor, and the Nine Rules Governing a Minor’s Agreement

A minor is defined, under Section 3 of the Indian Majority Act 1875, as anyone below the age of 18 — or below 21 if a court has appointed a guardian to manage that person, or a Court of Wards is managing their property (in easy language: normally you become an adult at 18, but if a court has had to step in to look after you or your property, that age moves to 21). Once someone is a minor, nine specific rules govern how the law treats any agreement they enter into.

  1. A minor’s agreement is void ab initio, meaning it is treated as having no legal existence at all right from the very moment it was made (in easy language: the law behaves as if the agreement never happened in the first place, not just that it later became invalid). This was settled in the landmark case of Mohiri Bibi vs Dharmodas Ghose, where a minor mortgaged his property to secure a loan of ₹20,000, of which only ₹8,000 was actually paid out to him; the Privy Council held that Sections 10 and 11 of the Act together make a minor’s contract absolutely void, and as a result, the money that had been advanced to the minor could not be recovered from him.
  2. The law of estoppel does not apply against a minor (in easy language: normally, if you make a false statement and someone relies on it, you are not later allowed to deny that statement was true — but this rule is set aside when the person who made the false statement was a minor). This was established in Leslie vs Shiell, where a minor fraudulently told a lender he was an adult in order to obtain a loan; the court held that the contract was still void, and the minor was not liable to repay the loan despite his own dishonesty about his age.
  3. There is no Doctrine of Restitution against a minor (in easy language: even where a minor has received some benefit or property under a void agreement, the courts generally will not force the minor to give it back).
  4. A minor’s agreement cannot later be validated simply by the minor confirming it once they become an adult; the law calls this confirming act “ratification,” and it is not permitted here — instead, an entirely fresh agreement, supported by fresh consideration, must be made after the person reaches majority (in easy language: you cannot simply say “I agree to it now that I am grown up” about an old childhood agreement; a brand new agreement, with something new being exchanged, has to be made instead). This was confirmed in Indran Ramaswamy vs Anthiappa Chettiar, where the court held that neither the original promissory note made during the person’s minority, nor a “fresh” note later executed to replace it, was valid.
  5. An agreement that is beneficial to a minor can be enforced BY the minor, even though the minor could not be sued on it themselves (in easy language: a minor is allowed to hold the other party to a deal that helps the minor, even though the minor cannot be forced to keep their own side of such a deal). This was illustrated in Roberts vs Gray, where a minor billiards player’s contract to tour and compete alongside a professional player was upheld as beneficial to the minor, since it effectively amounted to the minor receiving professional instruction.
  6. A minor can validly act as an agent on behalf of someone else, but the minor can never be held personally liable for any loss that results from their actions as that agent (in easy language: a minor can run errands or make deals on someone else’s behalf, but if something goes wrong, the minor personally cannot be blamed or made to pay for it).
  7. A minor’s liability for necessaries supplied to them can only be enforced against the minor’s own property, and never against the minor personally (in easy language: if a minor is supplied with things they genuinely need, like food or clothing appropriate to their situation in life, they can be made to pay for these out of any property they own — but they cannot be personally sued or imprisoned over the debt). What counts as a “necessary” depends on the minor’s own station and standard of living, as shown in Nash vs Inman, where eleven fancy coats bought by a minor who was already well supplied with clothing were held NOT to count as necessaries.
  8. A minor can never be adjudged insolvent (in easy language: because a minor's agreements are void from the start, the minor cannot owe the kind of enforceable debts that would let a court declare them bankrupt).
  9. When a minor and an adult jointly enter into an agreement together, only the adult party can be held liable under it, and the minor remains completely free of any liability arising from that same agreement.

Sound Mind [Sec 12]: capable, AT THE TIME of contracting, of understanding it and forming a rational judgment on its effect. A usually-unsound person CAN contract during a lucid interval; a usually-sound person CANNOT contract while drunk or delirious. Other disqualified persons: alien enemy (contracts suspended during war), foreign sovereigns/ambassadors, convicts (during imprisonment), insolvents, companies (only within their Memorandum), intoxicated persons.

CONCEPT

2.4 (cont’d) Free Consent ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Section 13 of the Act defines consent as the state where two or more persons agree upon the same thing in the same sense (in easy language: both sides must genuinely mean the same thing by the deal they are making, not just say similar-sounding words while actually picturing different arrangements in their heads). This point was illustrated in Foster vs Mackinnon, where a person signed a document believing it to be a guarantee, when it was in fact a bill of exchange; because the signer’s mind had never truly agreed to what he was actually signing, the transaction was held void from the very start.

Consent is only “free,” under Section 14, when it has NOT been caused by any of five factors that the law treats as corrupting genuine agreement: Coercion, Undue Influence, Fraud, Misrepresentation, or Mistake. Each of these five is explained below, one at a time.

Vitiating Factor 1 — Coercion [Section 15]

Coercion means committing, or threatening to commit, any act that is forbidden by the Indian Penal Code, or unlawfully detaining, or threatening to detain, someone’s property (in easy language: forcing someone into an agreement through an illegal act or an illegal threat, rather than letting them agree freely).

  • In Ranganayakamma vs Alwar Sett, a widow was forced to adopt a child under the threat that her deceased husband’s corpse would not be released for cremation unless she agreed; this was held to be coercion, making the adoption voidable.
  • In Ammiraju vs Seshamma, a threat to commit suicide was itself held to amount to coercion, even though suicide is a threat against oneself rather than against the other party.
  • In the Andhra Sugar Ltd. case, the court clarified that mere compulsion arising from the operation of law itself is NOT coercion — coercion requires an illegal act or threat, not simply the ordinary binding force of a valid law.
  • Under Section 19, the legal effect of coercion is that the resulting contract becomes voidable at the option of the party whose consent was obtained through it (in easy language: the person who was coerced gets to choose whether to walk away from the contract or keep it — the contract is not automatically cancelled on its own).

Vitiating Factor 2 — Undue Influence [Section 16]

Undue influence arises when one party is in a position to dominate the will of the other — because of real or apparent authority over them, or a relationship of trust between them, or because the other party’s mental capacity has been weakened by age, illness, or similar distress — and that dominant party uses their position to gain an unfair advantage (in easy language: one person has power or influence over another, and instead of respecting that trust, uses it to push the weaker person into an agreement that mainly benefits the stronger one). Once it is shown that such a dominant relationship existed, the burden of proving that undue influence was NOT actually used shifts onto the dominant party themselves, rather than staying with the person who was influenced.

  • Undue influence is legally presumed to exist in certain relationships by their very nature, including parent and child, guardian and ward, doctor and patient, solicitor and client, trustee and beneficiary, religious advisor and disciple, and an engaged couple.
  • In Mannu Singh vs Umadat Pandey, a disciple’s gift of his entire property to his religious guru, made in the hope of spiritual salvation, was held to be the product of undue influence.
  • Undue influence is NOT presumed, by contrast, in relationships such as landlord and tenant, debtor and creditor, or ordinarily between husband and wife — unless the wife is a “pardanashin” woman, meaning a woman who observes strict seclusion from contact with people outside her own household and is therefore considered less able to protect her own interests in dealings with outsiders.
  • In Inche Noriah vs Shaikh Alie bin Omar, an illiterate elderly woman’s gift deed transferring property to her nephew, who had been managing her affairs, was set aside by the court on the ground of undue influence.
  • Under Section 19A, the legal effect of undue influence is that the resulting contract becomes voidable at the option of the party who was influenced.

Vitiating Factor 3 — Fraud [Section 17]

Fraud covers a knowingly false suggestion, an active concealment of a fact, a promise made without any real intention of performing it, or any other act specifically designed to deceive — and critically, all of these must be done WITH THE INTENT TO DECEIVE the other party (in easy language: fraud is not just being wrong; it is deliberately lying, hiding something important on purpose, or making a promise you never meant to keep, all in order to trick the other side).

  • The Act specifically clarifies that mere silence about facts likely to affect someone’s willingness to enter a contract is NOT, by itself, fraud — unless the silence occurs where there was a duty to speak, or unless staying silent is itself equivalent to actually speaking under the circumstances.
  • In Peek vs Gurney, the non-disclosure of a company’s existing liabilities in its prospectus was held to amount to fraud, since investors were entitled to rely on a complete and honest picture of the company’s financial position.
  • In Bisset vs Wilkinson, an honestly held opinion about how many sheep a piece of land could support was held NOT to be misrepresentation, because it was a genuine opinion honestly given, not a false statement of fact made to deceive.

Vitiating Factor 4 — Misrepresentation [Section 18]

Misrepresentation covers an INNOCENT false statement — that is, a positive assertion made honestly but mistakenly, an unintentional breach of some duty that ends up giving one party an advantage without any real intent to deceive, or innocently causing the other party to be mistaken about the substance of the agreement (in easy language: misrepresentation is getting something wrong by honest mistake, with no intention to trick anyone, which is the key difference that separates it from fraud).

Vitiating Factor 5 — Mistake [Sections 20–22]

  • A mistake about the LAW OF INDIA does not make a contract voidable, because ignorance of one’s own country’s law is not accepted as an excuse (in easy language: you cannot get out of a contract just by claiming you didn’t know what Indian law said).
  • A mistake about a FOREIGN law, by contrast, is treated the same way as a mistake of fact, and can excuse a party, since nobody is expected to already know the law of every other country.
  • A BILATERAL mistake of fact, where both parties are mistaken about the same essential fact, makes the agreement VOID under Section 20 (in easy language: if both sides were genuinely wrong about the same key fact, there was never a true meeting of minds, so the law treats the agreement as if it never validly existed). This was illustrated in Raffles vs Wichelhaus, where both parties to a contract for the sale of cotton each had a different ship named “Peerless” in mind, with no way to know they meant different ships; the agreement was held void for lack of true consensus between them.
  • A UNILATERAL mistake, under Section 22, where only ONE party is mistaken, does NOT by itself make the contract voidable (in easy language: if only you were confused about something, and the other side genuinely wasn’t, the law generally still holds you to the deal).
⚡ SHORTCUT: Fraud = KNOWS it’s false. Misrepresentation = HONESTLY believes it’s true. Coercion = an ILLEGAL act/threat. Undue Influence = a DOMINANT RELATIONSHIP abused, no illegality required.

Concept Check 6 — Capacity and Free-Consent Vitiating Factors

GIVEN: (a) a 16-year-old fraudulently claims to be 19 and borrows money, then refuses to repay. (b) a religious guru persuades his disciple to gift his entire property for "salvation." (c) both parties to a contract believe a specific horse is alive, when in fact it died before the agreement was made.

STEP 1: (a) the law of estoppel doesn't apply against a minor — he can still plead minority despite his own earlier fraud (Leslie vs Shiell) → void ab initio, not liable.

STEP 2: (b) a dominant, fiduciary religious relationship exploited for unfair advantage (Mannu Singh vs Umadat Pandey) → Undue Influence, voidable.

STEP 3: (c) both parties mistaken about the very existence of the subject matter → Bilateral Mistake of Fact, void.

ANSWER: (a) Void ab initio (minor's agreement, Mohiri Bibi principle). (b) Voidable — Undue Influence. (c) Void — Bilateral Mistake [Sec 20].

CONCEPT

2.5 Quasi Contracts ★★★ HIGH

A Quasi-Contract is an obligation that the law itself creates and enforces even though the two parties never actually entered into a real contract with each other (in easy language: no one ever sat down and agreed to anything, but the situation is so similar to a contract that the law treats it as if one existed, purely to prevent one person from unfairly benefiting at another’s expense). The Act itself describes these as “certain relations resembling those created by contract.” A quasi-contract rests on principles of equity and justice, and the remedy available is compensation, not the kind of damages that would follow a genuine broken contract.

Five features distinguish a quasi-contract from a genuine one, and every one of them is worth remembering as a complete idea rather than a keyword.

  • A quasi-contract is imposed directly by law, rather than arising from any agreement the parties themselves made.
  • It is based on a legal duty that one party owes, rather than on any promise that was actually exchanged.
  • The right created is always a right to receive money, not to any other kind of performance.
  • The obligation is available only against a specific person or persons, not against the world at large the way certain property rights are.
  • Despite never being a real contract, it can still be enforced by filing a suit, in exactly the same way a genuine contract could be.

The Act recognises five distinct situations that are treated as quasi-contracts, each covered by its own section.

  1. Under Section 68, when necessaries are supplied to a person who is incompetent to contract, such as a minor, the supplier can recover the value of those necessaries — but only out of that incompetent person’s own PROPERTY, never from the person personally.
  2. Under Section 69, when a person who has some interest in a matter makes a payment, in good faith and not as a gift, in order to discharge another person’s existing LEGAL obligation to a third party, that person is entitled to be reimbursed by the party whose obligation was discharged (in easy language: if you step in and pay someone else’s legally-owed bill because you had a genuine stake in it being paid, honestly and not as a favour, you can claim that money back from the person whose bill it really was).
  3. Under Section 70, when one person lawfully does something for another, not intending to do it for free, and the other person actually enjoys the benefit of it, the person who did the act is entitled to compensation for it.
  4. Under Section 71, a person who finds goods belonging to someone else and takes them into their custody is treated by law in the same way as a person who has been formally entrusted with someone else’s property for safekeeping, which the law calls a “bailee” (in easy language: if you find a lost item and pick it up, the law holds you to the same standard of care as if the owner had deliberately handed it to you for safekeeping), and the finder is under a duty to make a genuine effort to locate the true owner.
  5. Under Section 72, a person to whom money has been paid, or goods delivered, by mistake or under coercion, is bound to repay or return them to the person who mistakenly paid or was coerced into paying.

Contingent Contracts [Section 31]

A Contingent Contract is defined by the Act as a contract to do, or not do, something if some event, COLLATERAL to that contract, does or does not happen (in easy language: it is a perfectly real, valid contract, but whether it actually has to be carried out depends on some separate, outside event that isn’t itself the main thing the contract is about). This is different from an absolute or unconditional contract, where performance does not depend on any such external condition.

Three things must all be true at once for a contract to count as contingent: a genuinely real contract must exist between the parties; the performance of that contract must depend on an event that is uncertain to happen; and that event must be collateral, meaning it stands apart from the contract’s own main subject matter, rather than being the main subject matter itself.

Sections 32 to 36 lay down five specific rules for how contingent contracts behave, and each rule is worth reading as its own complete idea.

  1. Under Section 32, when a contract is contingent on an event actually HAPPENING, it cannot be enforced until that event happens, and if the event later becomes impossible, the contract becomes void.
  2. Under Section 33, when a contract is contingent on an event NOT happening, it becomes enforceable the moment it becomes certain that the event will not happen.
  3. Under Section 34, when a contract depends on how a living person will behave in the future, that behaviour is treated as having become impossible the moment that person acts in a way that makes the specified behaviour impossible — for example, if A promises to pay B on the condition that B marries C, and C instead marries D, then the condition of B marrying C has become impossible from that point onward.
  4. Under Section 35, when a contract is contingent on a specified event happening within a FIXED period of time, it becomes void if that time expires without the event happening, or if the event becomes impossible before the time expires.
  5. Under Section 36, a contract that is contingent on an event that is impossible from the very outset is void, and this holds true regardless of whether either party actually knew about that impossibility at the time the agreement was made.
⚡ SHORTCUT: Quasi-Contract = law steps in, no real agreement ever existed. Contingent Contract = a genuinely real agreement, made conditional on an uncertain COLLATERAL event.

Concept Check 7 — Quasi-Contract, or Which Contingent-Contract Rule?

GIVEN: (a) A delivers goods to B, mistaking him for C; B consumes them. (b) A promises to pay B if a certain ship returns within a year; the ship is burnt within the year. (c) A promises to pay B ₹1,000 if B marries A's daughter C — but C was already dead when the agreement was made.

STEP 1: (a) goods delivered under a genuine mistake, consumed by the recipient → Quasi-Contract [Sec 72].

STEP 2: (b) contingent on the ship returning [event happening]; the ship's burning makes that impossible → contract becomes VOID [Sec 32].

STEP 3: (c) contingent on an event (marrying a person already dead) that was impossible from the very start → void regardless of either party's knowledge [Sec 36].

ANSWER: (a) Quasi-Contract, Sec 72. (b) Void, Sec 32. (c) Void, Sec 36.

CONCEPT

2.6 Performance of Contracts ★★ MED

Section 37 lays down the basic duty at the heart of every contract: the parties to a contract must either perform their respective promises, or at least offer to perform them, unless that performance has been dispensed with or excused under the Act or under some other law (in easy language: making a promise in a contract means you actually have to carry it out, or genuinely try to, not just agree to it and walk away). A promise generally continues to bind the representatives of a promisor who has since died, unless a contrary intention appears from the contract itself — EXCEPT where the contract required the promisor’s own personal skill, such as a contract to paint a picture, which cannot be enforced against the representatives at all, since nobody else can substitute for that particular person’s skill.

Offering, Refusing, and Delegating Performance [Sections 38–41]

  • Under Section 38, when a promisor genuinely offers to perform their promise, this is called a “tender of performance,” and if that tender is unfairly refused, the promisor is not liable for non-performance and does not lose any of their own rights under the contract — provided the offer was unconditional, made at a proper time and place, and gave the promisee a reasonable opportunity to verify the promisor’s actual ability and willingness to perform.
  • Under Section 39, if one party refuses to perform their promise ENTIRELY, the other party may choose to put an end to the contract altogether, unless that other party has, through their own words or conduct, signalled that they still accept the contract continuing.
  • Under Section 40, if a promise is of such a nature that only the promisor personally could have intended to perform it, then the promisor must perform it themselves; but where the promise does not require the promisor’s own personal skill or involvement, its performance may be delegated to someone else instead.
  • Under Section 41, once a promisee has accepted performance of the promise from a third person rather than from the original promisor, the promisee can no longer afterwards enforce that same promise against the original promisor.

Joint Promisors [Sections 42–45]

  • Under Section 43, when two or more persons have made a joint promise, the promisee is entitled to compel any ONE of those joint promisors to perform the WHOLE of the promise, rather than being limited to claiming only that one promisor’s own share.
  • Whichever joint promisor ends up actually performing the whole promise may then compel the other joint promisors to make an EQUAL contribution towards it, and if any one of the joint promisors fails to contribute their share, the resulting loss is shared equally among the rest.
  • Under Section 44, releasing one joint promisor from their obligation does not discharge the other joint promisors from theirs, and it also does not free the released promisor from their own duty to contribute to the others if called upon.

Time and Place of Performance [Sections 46–50]

  • Where a contract specifies no particular time for performance at all, the promise must be performed within a REASONABLE time, with what counts as reasonable depending on the facts of each case.
  • Where a time for performance IS specified, but no application by the promisee is needed to trigger it, the promise can be performed at any point during the usual hours of business on that specified day, and at the proper place for performance.
  • Where no particular place for performance has been fixed by the contract, it becomes the promisor’s duty to ask the promisee to appoint a reasonable place, and to then perform the promise at whatever place the promisee names.

Reciprocal Promises [Sections 51–54, 57]

A reciprocal promise is one where each party’s promise is made in exchange for the other party’s promise, so that the performance of one side is genuinely tied to the performance of the other.

  • Under Section 51, a promisor need not perform their own promise unless the other party to the contract is ready and willing to perform their reciprocal promise in return.
  • Under Section 52, where the order in which reciprocal promises are to be performed is fixed by the contract itself, they must be performed in that order; where no such order is fixed by the contract, they must be performed in whatever order the very nature of the transaction itself requires.
  • Under Section 53, if one party to a contract actually PREVENTS the other party from performing their promise, the contract becomes voidable at the option of the party who was prevented, and that prevented party is also entitled to compensation for any loss caused by the other party’s failure to perform.
  • Under Section 54, where reciprocal promises must be performed in a particular order, and the party who was meant to perform first fails to do so, that defaulting party cannot claim the performance of the later promise, and must instead compensate the other party for any loss caused by their own failure to perform.
  • Under Section 57, where a single set of reciprocal promises is partly legal and partly illegal, only the legal portion of that set is treated as a valid contract; the illegal portion is not enforceable.

Time as the Essence of a Contract, and Appropriation of Payments [Sections 55, 59–61]

  • Under Section 55, if it was genuinely intended by the parties that the contract be performed within a fixed time, and that time is not met, the contract becomes voidable at the option of the promisee (in easy language: if being on time was truly meant to be critical to the deal, missing that deadline lets the other party walk away from the contract entirely, not just claim compensation).
  • If, on the other hand, it was NOT intended that time be of such critical importance, then a delay does not make the contract voidable at all; the promisee’s only remedy is a right to compensation for any loss caused by that delay.
  • Under Section 59, when a debtor who owes several distinct debts to the same creditor makes a payment, the debtor’s own indication, at the time of paying, of which debt the payment should be applied to is what controls how that payment is appropriated.
  • Under Section 60, where the debtor gives no such indication at all, the discretion to decide which debt the payment should be applied against passes to the creditor instead.
  • Under Section 61, where neither the debtor nor the creditor has made any such appropriation, the payment must be applied to the debts in the order of TIME, starting with the debt that is oldest, and proportionately across debts of equal standing where relevant.

Concept Check 8 — Performance Rules in Action

GIVEN: (a) A, B, and C jointly promise to pay D ₹3,000; D wants to recover the full amount from just A. (b) A owes B on a certain promissory note falling due 1st June, among other debts; on 1st June A pays B exactly ₹1,000 with no other communication.

STEP 1: (a) Section 43 lets the promisee compel ANY ONE joint promisor to perform the whole promise.

STEP 2: (b) with no express indication, but circumstances clearly pointing to the one distinct debt of that exact amount falling due that day, the payment is applied to that specific debt [Sec 59].

ANSWER: (a) D may recover the full ₹3,000 from A alone; A may then seek equal contribution from B and C. (b) The ₹1,000 discharges the promissory note specifically.

CONCEPT

2.7 Indemnity ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Section 124 defines a contract of Indemnity as one where one party promises to save the other from loss caused to them, whether by the conduct of the promisor personally, or by the conduct of any other person (in easy language: one side agrees to cover the other side’s losses if something specific goes wrong, no matter who actually causes that loss). Only two parties are involved: the Indemnifier, who is the promisor giving the protection, and the Indemnity-Holder, who is the promisee receiving it.

Under Section 125, the indemnity-holder has four distinct rights they can rely on once a covered loss materialises.

  1. The indemnity-holder can recover any damages they were compelled to pay in a lawsuit that the indemnity covered.
  2. The indemnity-holder can recover the costs of defending such a suit, provided that defending it was not against the indemnifier’s own instructions, and that the defence was conducted prudently, as a reasonably careful person would have conducted it.
  3. The indemnity-holder can recover any sums paid under a compromise of such a suit, again provided that the compromise was reasonable and not against the indemnifier’s instructions.
  4. Where the indemnifier’s liability is absolute, the indemnity-holder can sue for specific performance of the promise, rather than being limited to a claim for damages.

This last point was clarified in the well-known case of Gajanan Moreshwar vs Moreshwar Madan, where the court held that once a liability has been INCURRED and has become ABSOLUTE, the indemnity-holder does not first have to pay it out of their own pocket before calling on the indemnifier — they may instead require the indemnifier to make that payment directly.

Guarantee [Section 126]

A contract of Guarantee is a contract to perform the promise, or to discharge the liability, of a THIRD person, in the event that third person defaults (in easy language: someone steps in and promises that if a borrower fails to pay or perform, they personally will cover it instead). Unlike indemnity, a guarantee always involves THREE parties: the Surety, who is the person giving the guarantee; the Principal Debtor, who is the person on whose behalf the guarantee is given; and the Creditor, who is the person to whom the guarantee is given.

Guarantees can be classified along three different dimensions: they may be RETROSPECTIVE, covering an existing debt, or PROSPECTIVE, covering a future one; they may be SPECIFIC, covering a single transaction, or CONTINUING, covering a whole series of transactions; and they may cover the ENTIRE debt or only a PARTIAL portion of it.

The surety’s liability has several defining characteristics worth holding in mind together as one idea: it is SECONDARY to the principal debtor’s own liability, meaning the debtor remains primarily responsible; it is CONTINGENT, since it only arises once the debtor actually defaults; it is CO-EXTENSIVE with the principal debtor’s own liability, meaning the surety cannot be made liable for more than the debtor themselves owes; and it may still be further limited by whatever specific terms the surety themselves agreed to.

The surety is also given a set of rights against three different parties, and it helps to keep these three groups distinct from one another.
