  • Against the principal debtor, the surety has the right of subrogation, meaning that once the surety pays the creditor, the surety effectively steps into the creditor’s own shoes; the right to be indemnified by the debtor for whatever the surety was made to pay; the right to insist that the debtor honour their own original obligation; and the right to any securities the debtor may have given.
  • Against the creditor, the surety has the right to require the creditor to proceed against the principal debtor first in certain circumstances; the right of set-off; and the right to the benefit of any securities the creditor holds from the debtor.
  • Against any co-sureties, meaning other people who have also guaranteed the same debt, the surety has the right to demand equal contribution from them.

A surety can be discharged from their liability in several distinct ways.

  • By proper notice.
  • By the surety's own death.
  • By novation, meaning the substitution of a new contract for the old one.
  • By the creditor varying the terms of the original contract without the surety's consent.
  • By the creditor releasing the principal debtor.
  • By the creditor doing something that impairs the surety's own eventual remedy against the debtor.
  • By any misrepresentation or concealment of material facts at the time the guarantee was originally formed.

Pledge [Sections 172–178]

A Pledge, under Section 172, is the bailment — meaning the delivery — of goods as security for a debt, or for the performance of some promise (in easy language: you physically hand over an item as collateral, without actually transferring ownership of it). The person who pledges the goods is called the Pawnor, and the person who receives them as security is called the Pawnee. Crucially, a pledge never changes who legally OWNS the goods — only who holds possession of them.

The pawnee’s rights are laid out across four consecutive sections, and each covers a distinct situation.

  1. Under Section 173, the pawnee may retain the pledged goods not only for the original debt itself, but also for the interest due on that debt, and for any expenses incurred in preserving the goods.
  2. Under Section 174, the pawnee may also retain the goods as security for SUBSEQUENT advances made to the pawnor afterward, unless the parties have specifically agreed otherwise.
  3. Under Section 175, the pawnee may recover any EXTRAORDINARY expenses incurred in preserving the goods, but importantly, the pawnee does NOT get a right to retain the goods specifically on account of those extraordinary expenses — only to be paid for them.
  4. Under Section 176, if the pawnor defaults on the debt, the pawnee has three options: to sue the pawnor for the debt while still retaining the goods as security; to retain the goods as collateral security and also sue for the debt; or to sell the goods after giving the pawnor reasonable notice, remaining entitled to claim any shortfall from the pawnor if the sale proceeds are insufficient, while also remaining liable to hand over any surplus if the sale proceeds exceed the debt.

Under Section 177, the pawnor retains a right to redeem the pledged goods even after defaulting, right up until the moment of actual sale, provided the pawnor pays any expenses that arose specifically because of that default. Under Section 178, a pledge made by a MERCANTILE AGENT who is in lawful possession of the goods, acting in the ordinary course of their business, is treated as being just as valid as if the true owner had personally authorised it — provided the pawnee accepted the pledge in good faith.

Agency [Sections 182–230]

Under Section 182, an Agent is a person who does any act for, or represents, another person — called the Principal — in that other person’s dealings with third parties (in easy language: an agent acts on someone else’s behalf, and whatever the agent properly does is treated as though the principal did it personally). Under Section 185, no consideration is necessary to create a valid agency relationship at all, unlike most other contracts.

Agency can be created in several distinct ways, and it helps to hold each of these as its own separate idea.

  • Under Sections 186 and 187, agency can be created by an express or an implied agreement between the parties; this includes Agency by Estoppel, where someone is prevented from denying an agency they allowed others to believe existed, Agency by Holding Out, where a person’s own conduct leads others to reasonably believe an agency exists, and Agency by Necessity, which arises in genuine emergencies where someone must act on another’s behalf without prior authority.
  • Under Sections 196 to 200, agency can also be created by ratification, meaning the principal later approves an act that was done on their behalf without prior authority — but this requires that the principal had full knowledge of the facts, that the ratification covers the WHOLE transaction and not just part of it, that no third party is damaged by it, and that the act itself was a lawful one that was genuinely within the principal’s own power to have authorised in the first place.
  • Agency can finally also arise simply by operation of law, without any express agreement or ratification at all.

Under Section 188, an agent’s authority extends to every LAWFUL thing that is necessary in order to accomplish whatever act they were actually authorised to do. Under Section 192, where an agent properly appoints a sub-agent, the principal becomes bound by that sub-agent’s acts just as if the sub-agent had been directly appointed by the principal themselves; but where a sub-agent is appointed IMPROPERLY, without proper authority to do so, the original agent alone remains responsible for that sub-agent’s conduct. Under Section 230, an agent is generally NOT personally liable on contracts they make on behalf of a disclosed principal, except in certain specifically presumed circumstances — such as where the agent is contracting on behalf of a foreign principal, where the agent does not disclose the principal’s name at all, or where the principal cannot themselves be sued.

⚡ SHORTCUT: Indemnity = TWO parties. Guarantee = THREE parties, liability CO-EXTENSIVE with the debtor's. Pledge = security through DELIVERY of goods, no ownership change. Agency = consideration is NOT required to form it at all.

Concept Check 9 — Indemnity, Guarantee, Pledge, or Agency?

GIVEN: (a) Mr. X lends ₹25,000 to Mr. Y; Mr. Z promises that if Y fails to repay, Z will. (b) B deposits jewellery with A as security for a loan A gives him. (c) P promises to cover Q against any losses from proceedings R might bring over a sum of money.

STEP 1: (a) X=Creditor, Y=Principal Debtor, Z=Surety — three named parties, one's specific default covered → Guarantee.

STEP 2: (b) goods (jewellery) delivered as security → Pledge; B is Pawnor, A is Pawnee.

STEP 3: (c) two parties, covering loss from a third person's (R's) conduct → Indemnity.

ANSWER: (a) Guarantee, (b) Pledge, (c) Indemnity.

CONCEPT

2.8 E-Contracts & E-Signature ★★ MED

Section 10A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, inserted by the IT (Amendment) Act, 2008, establishes that a contract formed through electronic means — where the proposal, its acceptance, and any revocation are all expressed electronically — is NOT unenforceable purely because it was carried out electronically rather than on paper.

Two roles are defined for the parties exchanging an electronic message: the “Originator,” under Section 2(za) of the IT Act, is whoever initiates or sends the message, and the “Addressee,” under Section 2(b), is whoever the message is actually intended for — and importantly, neither of these terms includes any intermediary who merely transmits the message along the way.

  • An Electronic Signature, under Section 2(p) of the IT Act, is the authentication of an electronic record by a subscriber using a specified electronic technique, which includes digital signatures as covered further under Sections 3 and 3A.
  • Under Section 5 of the IT Act, wherever a law requires something to be signed, that requirement is deemed satisfied if the document instead carries a valid electronic signature.
  • Under Section 85C of the Indian Evidence Act, courts are entitled to presume that the information contained in a valid digital signature certificate is true and correct, without needing separate proof.

Three distinct types of e-contract are recognised, and the difference between them lies in exactly WHAT ACT counts as the acceptance.

  1. In a Browse-wrap contract, simply continuing to use a website is treated as deemed acceptance of that website’s terms, without the user needing to take any separate, explicit action.
  2. In a Shrink-wrap contract, the act of opening a purchased product’s packaging is what triggers acceptance of the licence terms enclosed inside, even though the user could not see those terms before opening it.
  3. In a Click-wrap contract, acceptance requires an explicit “I agree” click, and critically, all the terms must be visible to the user before that click is made — this is what distinguishes it from shrink-wrap, where the terms stay hidden inside the box until after the product is already opened.

On the question of validity, the Indian Contract Act already recognises even purely oral contracts as valid, provided they involve free consent, lawful consideration and object, and are not expressly declared void — so there is nothing in principle that bars an electronic agreement from being valid too, as long as it possesses all the same essential elements. E-contracts are typically offered on a “take it or leave it” basis, with little real scope for the other party to negotiate their terms. This was addressed in LIC India vs Consumer Education and Research Centre, where the Supreme Court held that in such “dotted line” contracts, the weaker party genuinely has no real bargaining power — they can only accept the terms as offered or forgo the service entirely — and as a result, unfair terms embedded in such contracts can themselves be held void.

⚡ SHORTCUT: Browse-wrap = using the site IS acceptance. Shrink-wrap = opening the box IS acceptance. Click-wrap = an explicit "I Agree" click IS acceptance, with terms visible beforehand.

Concept Check 10 — Classify the E-Contract Type

GIVEN: (a) a user keeps browsing a website after its terms of use were revised, without any explicit action. (b) a buyer opens a software box, and the enclosed licence terms immediately bind them. (c) a user clicks "I Agree" after reviewing terms displayed on-screen before installing an app.

ANSWER: (a) Browse-wrap, (b) Shrink-wrap, (c) Click-wrap.

CONCEPT

2.9 Discharge of Contracts ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Discharge of a contract means the termination of the contractual relationship, the point at which the rights and obligations that the contract created come to an end (in easy language: the contract stops being a live, binding thing between the parties). The Act recognises six distinct ways a contract can reach this end point.

1. Discharge by Performance

This can happen through ACTUAL performance, where both parties genuinely fulfil their obligations exactly as the contract required, or through ATTEMPTED performance, also called tender, where a valid tender that is wrongly refused is treated in law as being just as good as actual performance.

2. Discharge by Agreement [Sections 62–63]

Five distinct routes fall under this heading, and each is worth holding as its own separate idea rather than blending them together.

  1. Novation means substituting an entirely NEW contract in place of the old one, whether between the same parties or different ones, and this requires the consent of ALL the parties involved — for example, if A owes a debt to B, and A, B, and C all agree that C will become the new debtor in A’s place, that is novation.
  2. Alteration means the parties to the contract stay exactly the same, but one or more of the contract’s own TERMS are changed by mutual agreement.
  3. Rescission means the cancellation of all, or some, of the terms of the contract, again by the parties’ mutual agreement.
  4. Remission means a promisee agreeing to accept LESSER performance than what is actually due under the contract, and importantly, no fresh consideration is required for this to be valid.
  5. Waiver means a party voluntarily giving up a right they were entitled to under the contract — for example, if B has engaged A to paint a picture for him, and B then tells A not to go ahead with it, A is no longer bound to perform, because B has waived his right to that performance.

3. Discharge by Lapse of Time

Under the Limitation Act, a debt or right that is never enforced within the time limit the law allows becomes “time-barred,” meaning it can no longer be enforced through the courts at all — for example, if no suit is filed to recover a particular debt within three years, that debt becomes time-barred and the contract is discharged on that ground.

4. Discharge by Operation of Law

Four distinct situations fall under this heading, each triggered automatically by law rather than by anything the parties themselves decide.

  • On the DEATH of a party, contracts requiring that party’s own personal skill come to an end, while other, ordinary contracts instead pass on to that party’s legal representatives.
  • On a party’s INSOLVENCY, their liabilities that existed before being formally adjudicated insolvent are discharged.
  • An UNAUTHORISED MATERIAL ALTERATION to a written contract — for example, changing the payment amount, the date, or the place of payment without the other party’s consent — discharges the contract.
  • Under MERGER, inferior rights held under one contract merge into superior rights created by a new contract — for example, when a part-time lecturer is made a full-time lecturer, their earlier part-time contract merges into, and is discharged by, the new full-time one.

5. Discharge by Breach, and 6. Discharge by Impossibility of Performance

A contract is also discharged by BREACH, which is covered fully in the next topic. Finally, a contract is discharged by IMPOSSIBILITY OF PERFORMANCE: an agreement to do something that is inherently impossible is void from the outset, because the law never compels anyone to do what genuinely cannot be done.

⚡ SHORTCUT: Novation = new contract replaces old. Alteration = same contract, changed terms. Rescission = simply cancelled. Remission = promisee accepts less. Waiver = promisee gives up the right entirely.

Concept Check 11 — Identifying the Mode of Discharge

GIVEN: (a) A, B, and C agree that C will now owe B the amount A originally owed, discharging A entirely. (b) A promises to paint a picture for B; B later forbids him from doing so. (c) a part-time lecturer's contract is superseded when they're made a full-time lecturer.

STEP 1: (a) a new debtor substituted with all parties' consent → Novation.

STEP 2: (b) the promisee voluntarily gives up their right to performance → Waiver.

STEP 3: (c) inferior rights merge into a new, superior set of rights → Discharge by Merger.

ANSWER: (a) Novation, (b) Waiver, (c) Discharge by Operation of Law (Merger).

CONCEPT

2.10 Breach of Contract & Remedies for Breach ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Breach of contract is the failure or refusal of a party to perform their obligation without any lawful excuse for doing so.

Two distinct types of breach are recognised, and the difference between them lies in WHEN the failure occurs relative to the date performance was actually due.

  • Actual, or Present, Breach is a failure to perform that occurs at the very time performance is due, or during the course of performance itself; it discharges the contract and gives the aggrieved party a right to sue.
  • Anticipatory, or Constructive, Breach happens when a party repudiates their liability BEFORE the time performance is even due, or disables themselves from performing through their own conduct — for example, if a person agrees to marry B, but then marries someone else, X, before the wedding date they had promised B, that is an anticipatory breach. Importantly, an anticipatory breach does NOT by itself discharge the contract; the contract is only discharged once the aggrieved party actually ACCEPTS the repudiation — until then, the contract continues in force and may still be performed.

Compensation Under Sections 73–75

  • Under Section 73, compensation is payable for loss or damage that arises NATURALLY, in the usual course of things, from the breach, or that both parties actually knew was LIKELY to result from it — but never for loss that is remote or only indirectly connected to the breach. This section also covers obligations resembling a contract that were never properly discharged.
  • Under Section 74, where the contract itself names a specific sum as a penalty for breach, the aggrieved party may recover REASONABLE compensation up to, but not exceeding, that named sum — and critically, this is recoverable WHETHER OR NOT the aggrieved party actually proves they suffered that much loss. The one exception is bonds given for a public duty, such as bail-bonds, where the FULL named sum must be paid regardless.
  • Under Section 75, a party who RIGHTFULLY rescinds a contract is entitled to compensation for any loss they suffer as a result of the contract not being fulfilled.

Five Remedies Available for Breach

  1. Suit for Rescission is a suit to cancel the contract, which frees the aggrieved party from any further obligations under it, and may also include compensation for damage they have already suffered.
  2. Suit for Damages is the most commonly used remedy, and it is compensatory in nature — it exists to compensate the aggrieved party for their loss, not to punish the party who breached the contract.
  3. Suit upon Quantum Meruit, literally meaning “as much as is earned,” entitles a party to payment proportionate to the work they actually completed — the right arises where a contract partly performed by one party has been discharged by the other party’s breach. The claim itself arises in three situations: where the contract is later discovered to be VOID; where something was done for another person without any intention that it be a free gift; or where one party refuses to perform their side of the contract.
  4. Suit for Specific Performance asks the court to order the actual promised act to be carried out, rather than simply awarding money, and it is granted only where monetary compensation would be an inadequate remedy, where there is no reliable standard by which to measure the actual damage suffered, or where compensation simply cannot practically be obtained at all.
  5. Suit for Injunction is a court order restraining a party from doing something they had specifically promised NOT to do; it may be temporary or permanent, and whether to grant it is left to the court’s own discretion.
⚡ SHORTCUT: Section 73 = compensation for natural/foreseeable loss, no pre-named figure. Section 74 = compensation capped at a pre-named penalty figure, awardable WHETHER OR NOT actual loss is proven — a nuance many miss, assuming Sec 74 always requires proof of loss.

Concept Check 12 — Section 73, Section 74, or Which Remedy?

GIVEN: (a) A contracts with B to pay B ₹1,000 if A fails to pay B ₹500 by a given day; A defaults. (b) A hires B's ship to carry cargo; B's ship never arrives, but A finds an equally advantageous alternative at some trouble and expense.

STEP 1: (a) a specific penalty figure (₹1,000) was pre-named in the contract → Section 74; B may recover reasonable compensation up to, but not exceeding, ₹1,000 — proof of actual loss is not strictly required.

STEP 2: (b) no pre-named penalty; A's genuine trouble and expense mitigating the loss is compensable as a natural, foreseeable consequence → Section 73.

ANSWER: (a) Section 74, capped at ₹1,000. (b) Section 73 — A recovers compensation for the trouble and expense incurred.

Module 2 — Trap Analysis

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: SECTION 25 EXCEPTIONS COUNTED AS ONLY THREE

THE TRAP: answering "no consideration, no contract" questions by naming only love/affection, past voluntary service, and time-barred debt.

THE TWIST: the Act recognises SEVEN exceptions in total — those three PLUS completed gifts [Explanation 1 to Sec 25], creation of agency [Sec 185], contract of guarantee [Sec 127], and remission [Sec 63].

WHY IT FOOLS: most study aids emphasise only the first three, since they're listed directly under Section 25 itself, while the other four are scattered across different Sections entirely.

THE FIX: if a question asks "how many exceptions," count all seven, not three.

MEMORY HOOK: "LOVE, PAST, TIME-BARRED, GIFT, AGENCY, GUARANTEE, REMIT" — seven words, seven exceptions.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: FRAUD AND MISREPRESENTATION SWAPPED

THE TRAP: an honestly-mistaken false statement labelled "Fraud," or a deliberately deceptive one labelled "Misrepresentation."

THE TWIST: the identical false statement can be either, purely depending on the speaker's state of mind. Fraud [Sec 17] = knowingly false, or without belief in its truth, WITH INTENT TO DECEIVE. Misrepresentation [Sec 18] = an innocent, honestly-believed false statement.

THE FIX: ask "did the speaker KNOW it was false?" Yes → Fraud. Honestly believed true → Misrepresentation.

MEMORY HOOK: Bisset vs Wilkinson (honest opinion, no fraud) vs Peek vs Gurney (concealed known facts, fraud) — same TYPE of act, opposite mental state.

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: SECTION 74's "PROOF OF LOSS" REQUIREMENT

THE TRAP: assuming a penalty named in a contract can only be recovered if actual loss is separately proven.

THE TWIST: Section 74 explicitly allows recovery of reasonable compensation up to the named sum "whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby."

THE FIX: Section 74 compensation is capped by the named figure, but not conditioned on proving actual loss the way Section 73 compensation effectively is in practice.

MEMORY HOOK: "74 has a NUMBER already named — the court just checks it's reasonable, not that loss was separately proven."

16 EXAM FACTS — INDIAN CONTRACT ACT, 1872

① Agreement = Offer + Acceptance. Contract = Agreement + Enforceability by law [Sec 2(e)/2(h)].

② Void Agreement [2(g)] = void ab initio. Voidable [2(i)] = at one party's option. Void Contract [2(j)] = valid, then later unenforceable.

③ Thirteen categories of expressly-void agreement, Sections 11/12→23→20→24→25→26→27→28→29→30→36→56→57.

④ Section 25's "no consideration, no contract" has SEVEN exceptions, not three: love/affection, past voluntary act, time-barred debt, gifts, agency, guarantee, remission.

⑤ Chinnayya vs Ramayya: consideration may move from the promisee OR any other person — a genuine departure from English privity.

⑥ Mohiri Bibi vs Dharmodas Ghose: a minor's agreement is absolutely void; the law of estoppel does not apply against a minor (Leslie vs Shiell).

⑦ Fraud [Sec 17] = knowingly false, intent to deceive. Misrepresentation [Sec 18] = innocently, honestly false.

⑧ Undue Influence [Sec 16]: burden of proving its ABSENCE falls on the dominant party.

⑨ Bilateral mistake of fact [Sec 20] → void. Unilateral mistake [Sec 22] → not voidable merely for that reason.

⑩ Quasi-Contract (Sec 68-72): law-imposed, no real agreement ever existed. Contingent Contract (Sec 31-36): a real agreement, conditional on an uncertain collateral event.

⑪ Indemnity (Sec 124): two parties. Guarantee (Sec 126): three parties, liability co-extensive with the debtor's.

⑫ Pledge (Sec 172): security through delivery of goods, no ownership change; pawnee may retain, sue, or sell (with notice) on default.

⑬ Agency (Sec 182): consideration is NOT required to create it [Sec 185].

⑭ Discharge: Novation (new contract), Alteration (same contract, changed terms), Rescission (cancelled), Remission (less accepted), Waiver (right given up).

⑮ Anticipatory breach doesn't discharge a contract by itself — only once the aggrieved party accepts the repudiation.

⑯ Section 73 = compensation for natural/foreseeable loss. Section 74 = compensation capped at a pre-named penalty, awardable whether or not actual loss is proven.

MODULE THREE OF FIVE · SECTION A · 20% · ≈10 MCQs

Sale of Goods
Act, 1930

Definitions, transfer of ownership, essential conditions of sale, conditions and warranties, performance of the contract, and the rights of an unpaid seller — built directly from the ICMAI Study Notes.

MUST NOT SKIP: Sale vs Agreement to Sell, Condition vs Warranty, and the Unpaid Seller's four rights against the goods — the most repeated question types in this module

10

Module Learning Objectives

After studying this module, you will be able to: understand the meaning of transfer of ownership; know the essential conditions of a contract of sale; appreciate the meaning of, and difference between, a condition and a warranty; understand the meaning of performance of the contract of sale; and know the rights of an unpaid seller.

Glossary — Module 3, in Plain Words

Legal English uses a lot of words you won't hear in daily conversation. Here's what the important ones actually mean, in the simplest words possible.

Vendor / VendeeOld words for Seller and Buyer. You'll see "Vendor" (seller) and "Vendee" (buyer) sometimes used instead of the plain words.
AscertainedPicked out and identified. "Ascertained goods" = the exact items have been separated from the rest and everyone agrees which ones they are.
UnascertainedNot yet picked out. "Sell me 10 mangoes from that basket of 50" — until 10 specific mangoes are separated, they're unascertained.
AppropriationThe act of setting aside specific goods for a specific contract, with both sides agreeing that these are "the" goods for this deal.
Deliverable stateGoods are ready to be handed over, exactly as agreed — nothing more needs doing to them first.
LienThe right to hold on to something (keep possession) until you're paid what you're owed for it.
RepudiateTo refuse to go ahead with the contract — to say "I'm treating this deal as over."
RescindTo cancel a contract, as if it never happened, and undo what's been done under it.
Merchantable / MerchantabilityGood enough quality to be sellable in the ordinary market — not damaged or useless.
WholesomeSafe to eat — used specifically for food items.
EncumbranceA hidden claim or charge on goods (e.g. someone else has a loan secured against them) that the buyer doesn't know about.
Caveat EmptorA Latin phrase meaning "let the buyer beware" — it's the buyer's own job to check the goods are what he wants, not the seller's job to point out every flaw.
Nemo Dat Quod Non HabetA Latin phrase meaning "you cannot give what you don't have" — if the seller doesn't truly own the goods, he generally can't pass good ownership to the buyer either.
Mercantile AgentA person authorised, in the normal course of business, to sell goods or raise money on goods on behalf of the real owner (e.g. a broker or commission agent).
WharfingerA person who runs a wharf (a loading dock by water) and stores goods there temporarily.
Bailee / BailorBailor = the person who hands over goods for safekeeping. Bailee = the person who receives and holds them temporarily, promising to return them later.
Symbolic DeliveryHanding over something that represents the goods (like a warehouse key) instead of the bulky goods themselves.
Constructive DeliveryNo goods physically move at all — a third party who is already holding the goods simply agrees to now hold them "on behalf of" the new buyer instead.
InsolventUnable to pay one's debts — financially unable to meet what is owed.
PerishableGoods that spoil or go bad quickly (fruits, vegetables, milk) if not sold or used soon.
StipulationA specific term or condition written into a contract.
Collateral (in "collateral term")Secondary, not the main point — something attached to the side of the main deal, not central to it.
Consignor / ConsigneeConsignor = the person sending goods. Consignee = the person the goods are being sent to.
Prima FacieA Latin phrase meaning "at first look" — true on the face of it, unless proven otherwise.
CONCEPT

3.1 Definition ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Sections 76 to 123 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 were repealed in 1930, and this content became the separate Sale of Goods Act, 1930, which took effect on 1 July 1930; the word “Indian” was later dropped from the Act’s own name on 22 September 1963. A sale is the only NON-REVERSIONARY transfer that occurs in business (in easy language: once goods are genuinely sold, they are gone for good — an absolute transfer, where the goods never come back to the seller the way they might under a lease or a loan).

Section 2 of the Act defines several terms that recur constantly throughout this module, and each is worth learning as its own precise idea rather than a vague impression.

  • Under Section 2(1), a Buyer is a person who buys, or agrees to buy, goods.
  • Under Section 2(13), a Seller is a person who sells, or agrees to sell, goods.
  • Under Section 2(2), Delivery is the voluntary transfer of possession of goods from one person to another.
  • Under Section 2(7), Goods means every kind of MOVABLE property, except for actionable claims and money; this includes stocks and shares, growing crops, grass, and anything attached to or forming part of the land that the parties have agreed will be severed from that land before the sale takes place.
  • Under Section 2(4), a Document of Title to Goods is a document such as a bill of lading, a dock warrant, a warehouse-keeper’s certificate, a wharfinger’s certificate, a railway receipt, or a warrant or order for the delivery of goods, which in law stands in for the goods themselves.
  • Under Section 2(6), Future Goods are goods that are to be manufactured, produced, or acquired by the seller only AFTER the contract of sale is actually made.
  • Under Section 2(10), the Price is the money consideration paid for the goods.
  • Under Section 2(11), Property means general ownership of the goods, and is distinct from merely holding possession of them.
  • Under Section 2(14), Specific Goods are goods that are identified and specifically agreed upon AT THE TIME the contract of sale is actually made.

Under Section 4(1), a Contract of Sale is a contract by which the seller transfers, or agrees to transfer, the property in goods to the buyer for a price (in easy language: this is the umbrella term covering every deal where ownership of goods changes hands for money, whether that change happens right away or later). This umbrella term itself splits into two distinct ideas under Section 4(3): a Sale, where ownership transfers IMMEDIATELY, and an Agreement to Sell, also called a Conditional Sale, where ownership instead transfers at a FUTURE date or once some condition is fulfilled — and it automatically becomes a sale once that future date arrives or that condition is actually met.

⚡ SHORTCUT: Sale = Executed contract, right in REM (against the goods themselves). Agreement to Sell = Executory contract, right in PERSONAM (against the person only) — this single distinction drives most of the nine differences between them.
BasisSaleAgreement to Sell
TransferOwnership transfers immediatelyOwnership transfers at a future date
TypeExecuted contractExecutory contract
Right createdRight in remRight in personam
Risk of lossBuyer bears it, even if seller still has possessionSeller bears it, even if buyer already has possession
ResaleSeller cannot resellA good-faith subsequent buyer gets good title; original buyer only sues for damages
Buyer's insolvencySeller must deliver to the official receiver (unless he has lien)Seller may refuse to deliver to the official receiver
Seller's insolvencyBuyer can claim the goods from the receiverBuyer only gets a rateable dividend on amount paid
TaxLiable for sales taxLiable for GST only once it "ripens" into a sale
★ EXAM TRICK: an Agreement to Sell isn't a weaker contract — it's simply timing-delayed; once its condition/date arrives, it automatically becomes a Sale without a fresh agreement.
CONCEPT

3.1 (cont'd) Types of Goods & Caveat Emptor ★★★ HIGH

Types of Goods: Existing Goods (owned/possessed by the seller now) — split into Specific (identified and agreed at contract time), Ascertained (identified AFTER the contract, per its terms), and Unascertained (not separately identified — described only generically, e.g. "25 of these 200 identical chairs"). Future Goods (to be manufactured/acquired later). Contingent Goods — a SUBSET of future goods, dependent on a contingency that may or may not happen (goods yet to arrive, future crops, unlaid eggs) — gives no right of action if the contingency never occurs.

Doctrine of Caveat Emptor ("let the buyer beware") [Sec 16]: the seller has NO obligation to point out defects in his own goods — the buyer must exercise care in selecting what he needs.

FIVE exceptions:

  1. Buyer discloses his particular purpose and relies on the seller's skill/judgment — an implied condition of fitness arises.
  2. Implied condition of merchantability when goods are bought by description.
  3. Condition of wholesomeness for foodstuffs.
  4. Where the seller commits fraud.
  5. Where a trade usage implies a condition.
⚡ SHORTCUT: Existing→Specific/Ascertained/Unascertained is about goods the seller ALREADY has. Future Goods (including the Contingent subset) are goods the seller does NOT yet have.

Concept Check 1 — Sale, Agreement to Sell, or Which Type of Goods?

GIVEN: (a) A agrees to sell B all the mangoes his orchard will produce next season. (b) A sells his car to B; ownership transfers to B on the spot. (c) A agrees to sell B 10 out of 100 identical bags of rice in his warehouse; the 10 bags haven't been separated yet.

ANSWER: (a) Future Goods (specifically Contingent, since the crop's existence is uncertain). (b) Sale (executed, immediate transfer). (c) Unascertained Goods (not yet separated/identified).

CONCEPT

3.2 Transfer of Ownership ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Sections 18 to 25 of the Act determine exactly WHEN property, meaning ownership, actually passes from the seller to the buyer (in easy language: this is the single most important question in the whole module, because whoever legally owns the goods at a given moment is also the one who bears the risk if something happens to them).

Seven rules together cover every situation the Act contemplates, and each is worth learning as its own distinct scenario.

  1. Under Section 18, for UNASCERTAINED goods, meaning goods not yet specifically identified out of a larger stock, property never passes to the buyer until those particular goods have actually been ascertained.
  2. Under Section 19(2), for SPECIFIC or already-ascertained goods, property passes at whatever moment the PARTIES THEMSELVES INTEND it to pass, and that intention is worked out by looking at the terms of the contract and the conduct of the parties. Where that intention is not clear from the contract, Sections 20 to 24 supply the default rules that follow.
  3. Under Section 20, where specific goods are already in a DELIVERABLE state, property passes the moment the contract itself is made, regardless of whether payment or delivery have actually happened yet.
  4. Under Section 21, where specific goods need something done to them by the seller in order to REACH a deliverable state, property only passes once that thing has been done AND the buyer has been given notice of it.
  5. Under Section 22, where specific goods need to be weighed, measured, or tested in order to ASCERTAIN THE PRICE, property only passes once that has been done and the buyer has notice of it.
  6. Under Section 23, for unascertained or future goods, property passes once goods matching the contract’s description are UNCONDITIONALLY APPROPRIATED to that contract, with the mutual assent of both parties — and delivering the goods to a carrier, without the seller reserving any right to dispose of them further, itself counts as such an appropriation.
  7. Under Section 24, for goods sent “on approval” or “on sale or return,” property passes when the buyer signifies their approval, or does some other act adopting the transaction, such as using the goods or reselling them, OR simply retains the goods beyond the fixed or reasonable time allowed for returning them, without actually rejecting them.

Risk, and the Perishing of Goods

Under Section 26, risk PRIMA FACIE follows PROPERTY, meaning ownership, rather than following mere possession (in easy language: the goods stay at the seller’s own risk right up until ownership actually transfers, and only then does the risk shift onto the buyer — and this happens REGARDLESS of whether the goods have physically been delivered yet).

  • Under Section 7, if specific goods had already perished, without the seller’s knowledge, BEFORE the contract was even made, the resulting contract is VOID.
  • Under Section 8, if specific goods perish AFTER an agreement to sell has been made, but before the risk has actually passed to the buyer, and this happens through no fault of either party, the agreement itself becomes VOID.
  • Both of these rules apply only to SPECIFIC goods that were identified at the time of contracting, not to generic or unascertained goods.
  • If the seller actually KNEW the goods had already perished before making the contract, he is estopped from disputing the contract on that ground; the buyer may then sue him for breach and claim damages, rather than the contract being void under Section 7.

Nemo Dat Quod Non Habet, and Its Six Exceptions

The doctrine of Nemo Dat Quod Non Habet means “none gives what he doesn’t have” (in easy language: as a general rule, someone who does not themselves own goods cannot sell you better ownership of those goods than they themselves actually had). This general rule exists to protect the true owner of goods from losing their property through no fault of their own.

Six recognised exceptions to this general rule exist, each protecting a good-faith buyer in a particular situation.

  1. Under Section 27, a sale by a MERCANTILE AGENT who is in lawful possession of the goods, and acting in the ordinary course of their business, is treated as valid even if that agent was not actually authorised by the true owner to sell.
  2. Under Section 28, a sale by ONE of several JOINT OWNERS, where that one owner is in sole possession of the goods with the permission of the other joint owners, is treated as valid.
  3. Under Section 29, a sale by a person who is in possession of goods under a VOIDABLE contract is valid, provided the sale happens before that voidable contract is actually rescinded.
  4. Under Section 30, a sale by a SELLER OR BUYER who remains in possession of goods AFTER an earlier sale or purchase has already taken place, made to a good-faith third party who is unaware of that earlier transaction, is treated as valid.
  5. A sale by ESTOPPEL is valid where the true owner’s own conduct led the buyer to reasonably believe that the seller genuinely had the authority to sell.
  6. A sale by a FINDER of lost goods, under Section 169 of the Indian Contract Act, is valid only where the true owner cannot reasonably be found, or refuses to pay the lawful charges owed, and where the goods are either perishable or the accumulated charges have reached two-thirds of their value; a sale by an official receiver or liquidator acting in an insolvency proceeding is valid on similar grounds.
⚡ SHORTCUT: Risk follows OWNERSHIP, not possession or delivery — a seller who still physically holds already-sold goods bears NO risk for their loss; a buyer who hasn't yet collected already-owned goods bears full risk.

Concept Check 2 — When Does Property Pass?

GIVEN: (a) A sells a specific, ready-to-use sofa to B; delivery and payment are both scheduled for next week; the sofa burns down in a fire at A's shop this week. (b) A sends 3 dozen sarees to B on approval, with 21 days to decide; B sells 2 dozen of them to C within the 21 days.

STEP 1: (a) the sofa was specific and already in a deliverable state — property passed the moment the contract was made [Sec 20], regardless of the later delivery/payment dates → the LOSS FALLS ON B, the buyer.

STEP 2: (b) reselling part of the goods is an act adopting the transaction [Sec 24(b)] → property passes to B at that point.

ANSWER: (a) B bears the loss — property had already passed under Section 20. (b) Property passes to B upon his act of reselling to C.

CONCEPT

3.3 Essential Conditions of a Contract of Sale ★★ MED

Under Section 4(1), a contract of sale of goods is a contract by which the seller transfers, or agrees to transfer, the property in goods to the buyer for a price.

Seven elements must all be present for a contract to qualify as a contract of sale.

  1. There must be TWO distinct parties, a Seller and a Buyer — one person cannot legally be both at once, except in specific court-ordered sale scenarios.
  2. The subject matter of the contract must specifically be GOODS, meaning movable property.
  3. There must be a genuine transfer of PROPERTY, meaning absolute ownership, and not merely a transfer of possession.
  4. DELIVERY of the goods may happen immediately, in instalments over time, or at some agreed future date.
  5. The PRICE must be paid in money consideration — a pure barter or exchange of goods for other goods is not a sale at all.
  6. The contract may be either ABSOLUTE or CONDITIONAL in nature.
  7. All the usual essentials of a valid contract under the Indian Contract Act still apply on top of these — free consent, capacity to contract, a lawful object, and so on.
⚡ SHORTCUT: If the "price" is another good rather than money, it's a BARTER/EXCHANGE, not a Sale of Goods contract at all — the presence of money consideration specifically is what makes Section 4 apply.
CONCEPT

3.4 Conditions & Warranties ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Under Section 12(2), a Condition is a stipulation that is ESSENTIAL to the main purpose of the contract, and breaching it gives the aggrieved party the right to REPUDIATE the contract entirely. Under Section 12(3), a Warranty is instead COLLATERAL to the main purpose of the contract, meaning it is a secondary term, and breaching it gives the aggrieved party only a claim for DAMAGES, never a right to reject the goods themselves.

Under Section 12(4), whether a particular stipulation counts as a condition or a warranty depends on the actual CONSTRUCTION of the contract, not on what label the parties happened to give it (in easy language: a term that the contract itself literally calls a “warranty” can still legally function as a condition, if it is genuinely essential to the contract’s main purpose). Both conditions and warranties may be EXPRESS, meaning explicitly stated by the parties, or IMPLIED, meaning built in by law unless the parties have specifically agreed otherwise.

Sections 14 to 17 imply seven distinct conditions into every contract of sale, unless the parties agree otherwise.

  1. The implied condition as to TITLE means the seller has the right to sell the goods in the first place.
  2. The implied condition as to DESCRIPTION means that where goods are sold by description, the goods actually delivered must correspond to that description.
  3. The implied condition as to SAMPLE means the bulk of the goods must match the sample shown, the buyer must be given a reasonable opportunity to compare the bulk with the sample, and the goods must be free of latent defects, meaning defects that a reasonable examination would not reveal.
  4. Where goods are sold by both SAMPLE AND DESCRIPTION together, the goods must correspond to BOTH the sample and the description, not just one or the other.
  5. The implied condition as to FITNESS or QUALITY arises only where the buyer discloses their particular purpose for the goods to the seller, and relies on the seller’s own skill or judgment in choosing suitable goods.
  6. The implied condition as to MERCHANTABILITY means the goods must be reasonably fit for the ordinary purposes for which such goods are normally used, in the sense of being genuinely acceptable in the market — for example, a watch that does not keep time is not merchantable.
  7. The implied condition as to WHOLESOMENESS applies specifically to foodstuffs, and requires the goods to be fit for actual human consumption.

Four distinct warranties are also implied into every contract of sale, unless the parties agree otherwise.

  1. The implied warranty of QUIET POSSESSION means the buyer’s peaceful enjoyment of the goods will not be disturbed by anyone with a better claim to them.
  2. The implied warranty of FREEDOM FROM ENCUMBRANCES means there is no hidden third-party charge or claim on the goods that the buyer was not told about.
  3. The implied warranty of FITNESS BY TRADE USAGE means an obligation annexed to the contract by the established custom of that particular trade.
  4. The implied warranty of DISCLOSURE OF DANGER means the seller must warn a buyer who is unaware of it if the goods being sold are inherently dangerous.
⚡ SHORTCUT: Condition breach → REJECT the goods AND claim damages. Warranty breach → damages ONLY, goods must be kept. A breach of condition CAN be downgraded and treated as a warranty breach (if the buyer chooses to keep the goods) — but a warranty breach can NEVER be upgraded into a condition breach.

Concept Check 3 — Condition or Warranty?

GIVEN: (a) A tells B his typewriter is "brand new"; B buys it, and it turns out to be old and repaired. (b) A sells B a car with a defective title he didn't know about — a third party later claims the car. (c) A sells B a car; B is later disturbed in his quiet enjoyment of it due to a hidden lien A never disclosed.

STEP 1: (a) a false description of the goods themselves → breach of the CONDITION as to description — B may reject and claim damages.

STEP 2: (b) the seller's right to sell was defective → breach of the CONDITION as to title.

STEP 3: (c) disturbed enjoyment due to an undisclosed encumbrance → breach of the WARRANTY of quiet possession / freedom from encumbrances — damages only, B keeps the car.

ANSWER: (a) Condition (description), reject + damages. (b) Condition (title). (c) Warranty (quiet possession/encumbrances), damages only.

CONCEPT

3.5 Performance of the Contract of Sale ★★★ HIGH

Under Section 31, performance of a contract of sale means, for the SELLER, the delivery of the goods, and for the BUYER, the acceptance of that delivery along with payment — both carried out in accordance with the terms the parties actually agreed to.

Under Section 32, delivery and payment are treated as CONCURRENT conditions unless the parties have agreed otherwise (in easy language: the seller must be ready and willing to hand over the goods in exchange for the price, and at the very same time, the buyer must be ready and willing to pay in exchange for possession — neither side has to go first). Section 2(2) recognises three distinct modes of delivery.

  • Actual, or Physical, delivery is where the goods are physically handed over from seller to buyer.
  • Symbolic delivery is where the seller hands over the MEANS of obtaining possession, such as the key to a warehouse, rather than the bulky goods themselves.
  • Constructive delivery is where a third party who is already holding the goods simply acknowledges that they now hold them on behalf of the buyer, with no goods physically moving at all.

Sections 31 to 44 lay down thirteen distinct rules governing delivery, and each is worth reading as its own complete idea.

  1. Under Section 33, delivery may take any mode the parties themselves agree to, or any mode that has the effect of putting the buyer in possession of the goods.
  2. Under Section 32, as already noted, delivery and payment are concurrent conditions unless the parties agree otherwise.
  3. Under Section 34, a PART delivery, made while delivering the whole quantity, has the SAME effect as a full delivery for the purpose of passing property in the goods — but if a part is delivered with the actual intention of SEVERING it from the rest, that part does not count as delivery of the remainder.
  4. Under Section 35, it is the BUYER’s responsibility to apply for delivery; the seller is not bound to deliver the goods unprompted.
  5. Under Section 36(1), the place of delivery follows whatever the contract specifies, and defaults to wherever the goods happen to be at the time the sale or agreement to sell was made if the contract is silent.
  6. Under Section 36(2), where no time for delivery is specified, delivery must happen within a REASONABLE time.
  7. Under Section 36(3), where goods are held by a third person, they are only treated as “delivered” once that third person ACKNOWLEDGES to the buyer that they are now holding the goods on the buyer’s behalf.
  8. Under Section 36(5), the cost of putting the goods into a deliverable state falls on the SELLER, while the cost of the buyer actually taking possession of them falls on the BUYER.
  9. Under Section 37, delivery of the WRONG quantity is handled in three ways: a short delivery lets the buyer either reject the goods entirely, or accept them and pay only proportionately for what was actually delivered; an excess delivery lets the buyer accept just the contracted portion and reject the rest, or reject the whole lot; and delivery of goods mixed with goods of a different description lets the buyer accept the conforming part and reject the rest, or reject everything.
  10. Under Section 38, delivery by instalments is not owed unless the parties specifically agreed to it, and whether a defective instalment lets the buyer treat the WHOLE contract as repudiated depends on the particular terms of the contract and the surrounding circumstances, rather than being an automatic rule either way.
  11. Under Section 39, handing goods over to a CARRIER or a wharfinger for onward transmission is prima facie treated as delivery to the buyer — but the seller must still make reasonable arrangements for the goods’ transit and custody, and must give notice about sea-transit insurance where that is customary, or else bear that particular risk themselves.
  12. Where the delivery point is far from the buyer, the risk of ordinary deterioration during that transit still falls on the buyer, once the seller has agreed to deliver the goods there.
  13. Under Section 41, the buyer has a right to EXAMINE the goods before being deemed to have accepted them.
⚡ SHORTCUT: Delivery to a carrier = prima facie delivery to the buyer (Sec 39) — this is a frequently-tested exception to the general rule that the SELLER bears the cost/risk of getting goods into deliverable shape.
CONCEPT

3.6 Rights of Unpaid Seller ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Under Section 45, a seller is treated as “unpaid” whenever the WHOLE price has not been paid, or whenever a bill of exchange or other negotiable instrument that was received as conditional payment has been DISHONOURED. A seller who has been only partly paid still counts as an unpaid seller for these purposes.

The unpaid seller’s rights fall into two groups: rights exercised against the GOODS themselves, and rights exercised against the BUYER personally.

Rights against the goods apply either where property has not yet passed to the buyer, or, in certain limited cases, even where it has.

  1. The right of Lien, under Section 47, is the right to RETAIN possession of the goods until payment, and it can be exercised where the goods were sold without any credit stipulation, where credit was given but that period has now EXPIRED, or where the buyer has become INSOLVENT. Three conditions must all be met: ownership must have already passed to the buyer, the seller must still be in POSSESSION of the goods, and the price must remain wholly or partly unpaid.
  2. The right of Stoppage in Transit, under Section 50, is the right to stop goods WHILE they are still in transit and to retain them until paid. This requires that the seller genuinely be unpaid, that the goods genuinely be in transit, that the buyer has become INSOLVENT, and that property in the goods has already passed to the buyer.
  3. The right of Resale, under Section 54, becomes available where the goods are PERISHABLE, where the seller had expressly reserved a right to resell on the buyer’s default, or where the seller, having already exercised either lien or stoppage in transit, gives the buyer notice of an intention to resell.
  4. The right of WITHHOLDING DELIVERY is available where property in the goods has not passed to the buyer at all.

Rights against the buyer personally give the unpaid seller four further remedies.

  1. A Suit for Price, under Section 55, becomes available once property has passed to the buyer and the buyer wrongfully refuses to pay for the goods.
  2. A Suit for Damages for Non-Acceptance, under Section 56, is available where the buyer wrongfully refuses to accept and pay for the goods.
  3. A Suit for Repudiation is available where the buyer repudiates the contract before the delivery date arrives; in that situation, the seller may either wait until that delivery date, or treat the contract as cancelled immediately and sue right away.
  4. A Suit for Interest, under Section 61, runs from whatever date the parties agreed to, or, if no date was fixed, from the date the seller actually notifies the buyer that interest is being claimed.
⚡ SHORTCUT: Lien needs the seller to still have POSSESSION. Stoppage in Transit needs the goods to be IN TRANSIT (out of the seller's hands, not yet reached the buyer) AND the buyer to be INSOLVENT specifically — not just any non-payment.

Concept Check 4 — Which Right Against the Goods?

GIVEN: (a) A sells goods to B on credit; the credit period expires unpaid, and A still has the goods in his own warehouse. (b) A sells goods to B; while the goods are with a carrier en route to B, A learns B has become insolvent. (c) A, having already exercised his lien on perishable goods, gives B notice of intent to sell them elsewhere.

ANSWER: (a) Right of Lien [Sec 47] — A still holds possession, credit period has expired. (b) Right of Stoppage in Transit [Sec 50] — goods are in transit, buyer is insolvent. (c) Right of Resale [Sec 54] — perishable goods, with proper notice given.

Module 3 — Trap Analysis

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: RISK FOLLOWS POSSESSION, NOT OWNERSHIP

THE TRAP: assuming whoever physically HOLDS the goods bears the risk of their loss.

THE TWIST: Section 26 makes risk follow OWNERSHIP (property), not possession — a seller who's already sold specific, deliverable goods bears NO risk even while they still physically sit in his shop; the buyer bears the loss.

THE FIX: ask "has PROPERTY actually passed?" not "who's holding the goods right now?"

MEMORY HOOK: "Risk follows the OWNER, not the WAREHOUSE."

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: LIEN AND STOPPAGE IN TRANSIT CONFUSED

THE TRAP: treating "unpaid seller retains/stops the goods" as one single right, regardless of where the goods physically are.

THE TWIST: Lien requires the seller to STILL HAVE POSSESSION. Stoppage in Transit specifically requires the goods to be IN TRANSIT — already out of the seller's hands, not yet reached the buyer — AND the buyer must have become INSOLVENT (mere non-payment isn't enough for stoppage).

THE FIX: "seller still holds the goods" → Lien. "Goods are with a carrier, buyer went insolvent" → Stoppage in Transit.

MEMORY HOOK: "Lien: goods never left. Stoppage: goods are on the road, chase them down."

⚠ TRAP

⚠ TRAP: A "WARRANTY" LABEL DOESN'T DECIDE THE OUTCOME

THE TRAP: assuming a term literally called "warranty" in a contract's text always gives only a damages remedy.

THE TWIST: Section 12(4) makes clear the classification depends on CONSTRUCTION of the contract, not its label — a term called "warranty" can still function as a legal Condition if it's essential to the contract's main purpose.

THE FIX: ask "is this term ESSENTIAL to the deal's main purpose (Condition), or just SECONDARY (Warranty)?" — never just read the label.

MEMORY HOOK: "The Act looks at what a term DOES, not what it's CALLED."

Module 3 — Comparison Tables

BasisCondition [Sec 12(2)]Warranty [Sec 12(3)]
NatureEssential to the contract's main purposeCollateral (secondary) to the main purpose
Remedy on breachRepudiate (reject) + damagesDamages only

★ EXAM TRICK: the label in the contract text is NOT decisive — Sec 12(4) looks at actual construction/substance.

12 EXAM FACTS — SALE OF GOODS ACT, 1930

① Sale = ownership transfers NOW, executed, right in rem. Agreement to Sell = ownership transfers LATER, executory, right in personam [Sec 4(3)].

② Specific Goods = identified at CONTRACT time. Ascertained = identified AFTER. Unascertained = not yet identified at all.

③ Caveat Emptor ("let the buyer beware") has FIVE exceptions: disclosed purpose+skill reliance, merchantability, wholesomeness, fraud, trade usage.

④ Risk follows OWNERSHIP [Sec 26], not possession — a seller can bear zero risk while still holding sold goods.

⑤ Nemo Dat Quod Non Habet has SIX exceptions: mercantile agent, joint owner, voidable-contract possessor, seller/buyer in possession after sale, estoppel, finder of goods.

⑥ Condition [Sec 12(2)] = essential, breach → reject + damages. Warranty [Sec 12(3)] = collateral, breach → damages only. The contract's LABEL doesn't decide which — construction does [Sec 12(4)].

⑦ Seven implied conditions [Sec 14-17]: title, description, sample, sample+description, fitness, merchantability, wholesomeness.

⑧ Four implied warranties: quiet possession, freedom from encumbrances, fitness by trade usage, disclosure of danger.

⑨ Delivery to a carrier is prima facie deemed delivery to the BUYER [Sec 39].

⑩ Unpaid Seller [Sec 45]: whole price unpaid, OR a conditional-payment instrument dishonoured — even a partly-paid seller still counts.

⑪ Lien needs continued POSSESSION. Stoppage in Transit needs goods IN TRANSIT + buyer INSOLVENT. Resale needs perishable goods, a reserved right, or notice after lien/stoppage.

⑫ Three delivery modes: Actual (physical handover), Symbolic (means of possession, e.g. a key), Constructive (third party acknowledges holding for the new buyer).

Negotiable
Instruments Act, 1881

Characteristics of negotiable instruments, the three key instruments (promissory note, bill of exchange, cheque), their differences, cheque crossing, and dishonour of cheques under Section 138 — built directly from the ICMAI Study Notes.

MUST NOT SKIP: the three-way comparison table and Section 138's five ingredients — the most repeated question types in this module

10

Module Learning Objectives

After studying this module, you will be able to: know the meaning and characteristics of negotiable instruments; appreciate the various types including bill of exchange, promissory note, and cheque; understand the difference between them; appreciate the different types of crossing; and understand the meaning and possible reasons for dishonour of cheques.

Glossary — Module 4, in Plain Words

The important words from this module, explained simply.

NegotiableCan be transferred from one person to another, simply by handing it over or signing it over.
InstrumentA written document that creates a right for someone — a piece of paper representing money owed.
DrawerThe person who creates/writes the cheque or bill and gives the payment order.
DraweeThe person (or bank) told to make the payment.
PayeeThe person who is supposed to receive the money.
MakerThe person who writes and signs a promissory note, promising to pay.
EndorsementSigning the back of an instrument to transfer it to someone else.
Holder in due courseSomeone who honestly received the instrument, paid a real value for it, before it was overdue, without knowing of any problem with it.
DishonourWhen a bank refuses to pay a cheque — most commonly because there isn't enough money in the account.
Crossing (a cheque)Drawing two lines across the front of a cheque, which means it can only be paid into a bank account, never handed out as cash over the counter.
BearerWhoever is physically holding the instrument — a "bearer" cheque can be cashed by anyone holding it.
Order (instrument payable "to order")Payable specifically to the named person, or to whoever THAT person formally transfers it to.
Grace periodA few extra days allowed before an instrument is officially treated as due/overdue.
Inchoate InstrumentAn instrument that's signed but left incomplete in some way (e.g. the amount is left blank), to be filled in later.
Ambiguous InstrumentAn instrument written in a confusing way that could be read as either a promissory note or a bill of exchange.
EscrowSomething handed over on the condition it's only used for a specific, agreed purpose.
Truncated ChequeA cheque converted into an electronic image during clearing, instead of physically moving the paper cheque around.
Interim CompensationMoney a court orders paid early on in a case, before the case is even fully decided.
CONCEPT

4.1 Characteristics of Negotiable Instruments ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Under Section 13, a Negotiable Instrument is a promissory note, bill of exchange, or cheque, payable either to order or to bearer. A holder of such an instrument acquires genuine property in it if they take it in good faith and for value, DESPITE any defect in the person who transferred it to them having had a defective title themselves — a key departure from the ordinary rules governing the transfer of property.

Four characteristics define what makes an instrument negotiable in this special legal sense.

  1. It has FREE AND INNUMERABLE TRANSFER, meaning it passes from person to person by delivery, or by endorsement and delivery together, and can keep being transferred like this indefinitely until it reaches maturity.
  2. It has FREEDOM FROM DEFECTS, meaning a HOLDER IN DUE COURSE gets good title regardless of any earlier defect in the chain of ownership, provided they took the instrument FOR CONSIDERATION, BEFORE its MATURITY, and WITHOUT NOTICE of any defect in the title.
  3. The holder may sue on the instrument in their OWN name, without needing anyone else’s involvement.
  4. SPECIAL PRESUMPTIONS apply under Sections 118 and 119 unless they are actually disproved: every instrument is presumed to have been made or transferred for consideration; a dated instrument is presumed to have been made on that stated date; a bill is presumed to have been accepted within a reasonable time; every transfer is presumed to have happened before maturity; endorsements are presumed to appear in the order they were actually made; a lost instrument is presumed to have been duly stamped; the holder is presumed to be a holder in due course; and once protest is proved, dishonour itself is presumed. If the instrument was obtained from its lawful owner or custodian by an offence, by fraud, or for unlawful consideration, this burden REVERSES — it is then the HOLDER who must prove they are a holder in due course.

Share certificates accompanied by blank transfer deeds, deposit receipts, and mate’s receipts are NOT negotiable instruments, despite sometimes being treated informally as if they were.

Negotiable instruments fall into two broad types: those negotiable by STATUTE, meaning the three instruments specifically named in Section 13, and those negotiable by CUSTOM or USAGE, such as dividend warrants, circular notes, and bearer debentures, which are not named in the Act itself but are treated as negotiable because trade custom has made them so.

Eight further classifications apply across negotiable instruments generally, and each pairs off two contrasting types.

  1. A BEARER instrument is payable to whoever physically holds it, or to whoever it was last endorsed in blank to, while an ORDER instrument is payable to a specifically named person, with no restriction on transferability.
  2. An INLAND instrument is both drawn AND made payable in India, or drawn on a person resident in India, while a FOREIGN instrument is any instrument that is not inland — and critically, protest for dishonour is COMPULSORY for a foreign bill, unlike an inland bill, where protest is merely optional under Section 104.
  3. A DEMAND instrument has no time specified for payment, and a cheque is ALWAYS a demand instrument, while a TIME instrument is payable only after a specified period or specified event. Under Section 21, the expressions “at sight” or “on presentation” on a promissory note or bill of exchange also mean payable on demand — “on demand” is the phrase usually found in a promissory note, while “at sight” is usually found in a bill of exchange.
  4. A GENUINE instrument involves real consideration, an ACCOMMODATION instrument involves no real consideration at all, and a FICTITIOUS instrument is one where the drawer or payee named is not a real person — if BOTH the drawer and payee of a bill are fictitious, the acceptor still remains liable to a holder in due course who can show that the supposed drawer’s signature and the first payee’s signature are in the same handwriting.
  5. A CLEAN instrument has no documents attached to it, while a DOCUMENTARY instrument has title documents attached.
  6. An AMBIGUOUS instrument is one that, due to faulty drafting, could be read as either a promissory note or a bill of exchange, and it is for the HOLDER to decide how it should be treated — and where the figures and the words on such an instrument conflict, the WORDS control over the figures.
  7. An INCHOATE instrument is one that is signed but left incomplete in some way, and the person who signed it remains liable up to whatever amount the stamp affixed to it could legally cover.
  8. An ESCROW instrument is one delivered conditionally, for a special or collateral purpose, and no liability arises under it at all if that condition is never actually met.
⚡ SHORTCUT: A Holder in Due Course needs THREE things together: consideration paid, acquired BEFORE maturity, and NO NOTICE of any defect — missing any one of the three breaks the protection.

4.1 (cont’d) Parties & Capacity

Several distinct roles can appear across the various parties to a negotiable instrument, and each carries its own precise meaning.

  • The Drawer is the maker of the instrument.
  • The Drawee is the person directed to make the payment.
  • A Drawee in Case of Need is a backup name that can be approached if the main drawee fails to pay; under Section 115, the bill is not treated as dishonoured unless even THIS backup person also refuses to pay, and under Section 116, this backup drawee may accept and pay the bill without any previous protest.
  • The Acceptor is the drawee, once they have signed their assent to the instrument.
  • An Acceptor for Honour is someone who accepts a protested bill specifically to protect the honour of the drawer or an endorser; if it is not specified whose honour is being protected, it is presumed to be the drawer’s.
  • The Payee is the person meant to receive payment.
  • The Holder is whoever is entitled, in their own name, to possess the instrument and to recover its amount; under Section 8, even after an instrument is lost or destroyed, whoever was entitled to it at that time continues to be treated as its “holder.”

On the question of capacity, a party who is themselves incompetent to contract creates a VOID agreement only AGAINST THEMSELVES — the instrument remains fully valid against every other party who was competent.

  • A MINOR cannot be personally bound by a negotiable instrument, but a minor CAN draw, endorse, deliver, or negotiate one in a way that binds ALL the OTHER parties to it; the minor’s own estate, rather than the minor personally, remains liable for necessaries.
  • A CORPORATION can be a party to a negotiable instrument only if its own Articles of Association authorise this; otherwise, doing so is ultra vires and beyond its powers.
  • An AGENT, under Section 27, must clearly sign in a representative capacity, such as “for ABC Ltd,” rather than simply signing as “A, manager” — failing to do this makes the agent PERSONALLY liable on the instrument.
  • A LEGAL REPRESENTATIVE, under Section 30, who signs an instrument on behalf of someone who has died, creates PERSONAL liability for themselves unless that liability is clearly and expressly limited to the deceased person’s estate.
⚡ SHORTCUT: An agent who signs just their own name plus a title ("A, Manager") is PERSONALLY liable; signing "for [Company]" avoids personal liability — the exact wording of the signature is the entire test.
CONCEPT

4.2 Definitions of Promissory Note, Bill of Exchange & Cheque ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC

Under Section 4, a Promissory Note is a written instrument, distinct from a bank note or currency note, containing an UNCONDITIONAL undertaking, SIGNED BY THE MAKER, to pay a certain sum only to, or to the order of, a certain person, or to the bearer of the instrument.

A promissory note involves only TWO parties, the Maker and the Payee, and it must satisfy ten distinct requisites.

  1. It must be in writing.
  2. It must contain an express UNDERTAKING to pay.
  3. That undertaking must be UNCONDITIONAL.
  4. It must be signed by the maker.
  5. It must specify a CERTAIN sum.
  6. It must promise payment in money only.
  7. Both the maker and the payee must be certain, identifiable persons.
  8. It must be stamped under the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, since an unstamped note is inadmissible in court and no suit can be brought on it.
  9. It must contain a date.
  10. The limitation period for filing a suit on it is THREE YEARS from its execution or from any later acknowledgment of the debt.

Under Section 5, a Bill of Exchange is a written instrument containing an UNCONDITIONAL ORDER, signed by the maker, directing a certain person to pay a certain sum only to, or to the order of, a certain person, or to the bearer.

A bill of exchange involves THREE parties — Drawer, Drawee, and Payee — and must satisfy nine requisites.

  1. It must be unconditional, though the acceptor or an endorser may still attach their own separate conditions to their own liability.
  2. It must be payable in money only.
  3. It must state a certain amount.
  4. It must indicate a certain time for payment.
  5. The word "order" here means a request, not literally a command.
  6. The drawer's signature is essential.
  7. The drawee must be named or otherwise identifiable.
  8. It must specify a date and place.
  9. It must be stamped under the Indian Stamp Act, 1899.

Under Section 6, a Cheque is a bill of exchange drawn on a SPECIFIED BANKER, payable on DEMAND — this definition also extends to a truncated cheque’s electronic image, and to an electronic cheque.

A cheque adds two further qualifications beyond an ordinary bill: it is always drawn on a specified banker, and it is always payable on demand. It involves three parties — the Drawer, who is the bank's own customer, the Drawee, who is the bank itself, and the Payee.

It must satisfy seven requisites:

  1. It must be a written order.
  2. It must be unconditional.
  3. It must be signed by the maker.
  4. The amount must be stated in BOTH figures and words.
  5. It may be made payable to bearer, to order, or to self.
  6. It must contain a date.
  7. The payee must be a certain, identifiable person.

On the question of the GRACE PERIOD, instruments payable otherwise than on demand are given THREE days of grace before they fall due. A cheque, any demand instrument, or an instrument with no time mentioned at all is NOT entitled to this grace period. A note or bill payable on a specified day, “after sight,” or on a certain event IS entitled to it. If the resulting due date falls on a public holiday, the instrument instead becomes due on the immediately preceding business day. Where an instrument is payable by instalments, each instalment falls due three days after the date fixed for paying it; and if the calendar month in which the period is to end has no day corresponding to the start date, the period instead ends on the last day of that month.

Payment in due course, which discharges the instrument entirely, requires five conditions to all be met together.

  1. The payment must match the instrument's apparent tenor, so paying before maturity does not count.
  2. It must be made to the drawee or acceptor, in genuine MONEY terms, whether cheque or currency, and never forced into some other mode of payment without the payee's consent.
  3. It must be made to whoever is actually in possession of the instrument AND entitled to receive payment on it.
  4. It must be made in good faith and without negligence — if a cheque bears the drawer’s forged signature, payment on it is NOT payment in due course unless the banker exercised the necessary care.
  5. There must have been no reasonable ground to doubt that the person receiving payment was actually entitled to it.
⚡ SHORTCUT: Promissory Note = an UNDERTAKING (a promise) by the maker himself. Bill of Exchange/Cheque = an ORDER by the drawer, directing someone ELSE (the drawee) to pay — this single distinction (promise vs order) explains why a Note has 2 parties and a Bill/Cheque has 3.

Concept Check 1 — Note, Bill, or Cheque?

GIVEN: (a) A writes and signs a document promising to pay B ₹50,000, no bank involved. (b) A orders his bank to pay C ₹10,000 on demand. (c) A directs B (not a bank) to pay C ₹20,000 after 60 days.

ANSWER: (a) Promissory Note (a personal undertaking, no third party directed). (b) Cheque (drawn on a specified banker, payable on demand). (c) Bill of Exchange (an order directing a non-bank third party, with a specified future time).

4.3 Difference Between Promissory Note, Bill of Exchange & Cheque ★★★ HIGHEST-VALUE TOPIC
